papers_seen.author: Frazier
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically proven family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into compact students. KD reduces inference cost and memory and supports a wide range of transfer targets and training regimes. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and selection, and design choices; for robust, fair, and production-ready compression it should be integrated with complementary techniques and targeted safeguards.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers information at multiple levels—soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational structure, or synthesized examples—and can be organized in diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free regimes). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design, KD routinely produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. However, KD’s success is strongly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and calibration, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and match of distillation data (or quality of synthetic surrogates), and careful objective and pipeline design to avoid propagating teacher errors or degrading long‑tail behaviour. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline, not a universal panacea.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied collection of techniques for transferring information from large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, graphs, retrieval, and multimodal problems, distillation methods—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and representation-level imitation, curriculum strategies, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enable deployable models that trade modest accuracy loss for substantial gains in latency, memory, and energy use. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers and capacities, and how to prepare data), but success requires managing failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, and sensitivity to distillation data. This synthesis summarizes what the provided literature reports about methods, mechanisms, applications, best practices, and open problems for KD-based model compression.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical toolbox for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. The field encompasses a diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational maps, contrastive signals), multiple training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, multi-teacher and ensemble schemes), and data strategies that include data-driven, synthetic, and data-free approaches. KD is routinely integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, generative models, recommender and graph systems). Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the distillation signal and its alignment, and the availability and curation of data; remaining challenges include preserving low-frequency behaviors, avoiding transfer of teacher biases, and maintaining robustness under distribution shift and limited-data regimes. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an overall compression pipeline with task-aware signal selection, careful teacher–student co-design, and targeted mitigations for privacy, fairness, and domain shift.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically supported approach for producing compact, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods — including soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online/self-distillation, and data-free or adversarial synthesis — enable substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. The effectiveness of KD is strongly context dependent: it hinges on what signals are transferred, teacher–student design and capacity alignment, data availability (or synthesis), and integration with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all solution. Remaining research and engineering challenges include robust and privacy-preserving distillation under data scarcity, improved methods for heterogeneous teacher–student mappings, and methods to avoid propagating teacher biases or damaging long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, multimodal, and graph tasks. When combined with architecture-aware design, layer- and feature-level objectives, adversarial or relational losses, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, NAS), KD enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss and can sometimes improve generalization. KD also faces clear limits—teacher bias, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and optimization instability—that require task-aware curricula, multi-teacher or ensemble strategies, and careful selection of distilled signals. This paper argues that KD should be the first-line instrument in compression toolkits for deep learning and NLP, provided practitioners adopt principled protocols that address known failure modes and integrate KD with complementary methods for the target deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models by transferring behavior from larger teacher models. When used as a configurable, task- and deployment-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD routinely reduces latency and memory while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Its practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and complementary compression primitives; persistent challenges include bias transfer, handling low-frequency phenomena, distribution shift, and automating signal selection.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD methods—ranging from soft‑logit matching to intermediate‑feature and attention transfers, adversarial or contrastive objectives, and multi‑teacher schemes—regularly enable large reductions in inference cost and parameter footprint while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD’s effectiveness is strongly dependent on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and optimization dynamics; therefore, reliable compression in practice requires combining KD with task‑aware design choices and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis) and explicit mitigation strategies for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and deployment‑specialized models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Methods include matching soft logits, aligning intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and online protocols, and data‑aware or data‑free variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable tool within an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation, rare‑token degradation, and distribution shift. Practical deployments therefore combine careful selection of transfer targets, layer and projector design, curricula and data synthesis, and complementary compression primitives while monitoring robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Cain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD spans output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocol variants such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, and privacy-aware workflows. In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and must be tailored to teacher/student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; while empirical results across modalities often show students can recover much of teacher performance, important challenges remain in handling capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias and robustness, and formal theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Key
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger, often ensemble, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at the logit level, at intermediate representation and attention levels, and via relational or contrastive objectives; they are routinely combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis. Empirically, well-designed distillation pipelines can produce compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance, enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy and device constraints. Success depends on choices about what and how to transfer, the quality and alignment of teacher and student, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data; important open problems remain around distribution shift, bias/fairness transfer, low-frequency behavior, and principled theoretical understanding.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative, and federated settings, KD has been applied to reduce latency and memory, enable on-device or privacy-sensitive deployment, and in some cases improve robustness or calibration. The field offers a broad toolkit—logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature/attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free or generator-assisted distillation, and ensembles or self-distillation—that practitioners combine with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical success is widespread but conditional: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and nature of distillation data, and task-aware choices about what and how to transfer. Persistent challenges include teacher–student mismatch, optimization gaps, distributional shift, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, and privacy/fairness trade-offs. Current research directions emphasize joint optimization of compression primitives, federated and cross‑modal distillation, improved data-free protocols, and automated teacher–student matching.

papers_seen.author: Bishop
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for producing compact, faster models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, retrieval, and generative tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher schemes—have been developed and combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of transferred errors and rare-output degradation. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, practical guidance, and open challenges for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Ortega
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used approach for producing compact models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. It offers multiple mechanisms (soft-targets, intermediate representation matching, attention- or channel-wise transfers, multi-teacher and data‑free variants) that, when combined with complementary compression techniques, can yield substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss. However, KD’s effectiveness is highly dependent on task, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints; consequently, it should be treated as an adaptable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. The literature defines a rich set of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive objectives) and training protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free/adversarial generation). KD is often combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering (projector adapters, curriculum/sample selection, multi-teacher weighting) to produce favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. Empirically, KD recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities, but its success is context-dependent and limited by teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution shift, and risks of propagating teacher biases or poor modeling of rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and employs targeted mitigations (multi-teacher schedules, projector layers, data synthesis/adversarial generation, privacy-aware protocols) to address concrete deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — A Task‑Aware, Integrative Position for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and widely adopted family of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the functionality of larger teachers while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, ranking and multimodal tasks shows KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs. However, KD has documented limits — dependence on teacher quality and student capacity, sensitivity to data availability and distribution shift, the risk of propagating teacher artifacts, and difficulty preserving low‑frequency or structured behaviors — that mean it should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone panacea. For robust, fair, and hardware‑aware deployment, practitioners should combine KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), task‑aware selection of distilled signals (logits, features, attention/relational objectives), careful teacher–student co‑design, and data strategies that address scarcity, privacy, and long‑tail phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Webb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Sensitive Toolkit for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger teachers to smaller students, but its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to train, and how to integrate complementary compression methods. When designed as part of a task-aware pipeline—with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and privacy or fairness constraints—KD yields deployable models that retain much of teacher performance; treated naively it can propagate errors and fail under data- or capacity-mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable paradigm for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when its objectives, data strategies, and student architectures are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of transferred biases and robustness gaps. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving much of the original performance. KD operates at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals) and across multiple training regimes (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free/synthetic data). Empirical work across vision, speech, and language shows KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs when combined with appropriate architecture alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical application treats KD as a configurable, context‑sensitive element of an integrated compression pipeline; its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and complexity, and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Lara
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Core for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported family of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. As a practical engineering tool, KD reliably reduces inference cost, memory use, and latency across modalities while often preserving most of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a universal or standalone solution: its effectiveness is conditional on teacher and student design, data regimes, choice of distilled signals, and careful integration with complementary compression primitives and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Treated as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline, KD offers the best balance between efficiency and fidelity for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. A rich palette of distillation targets and training regimes—soft logits, intermediate representations, attention patterns, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline that aligns teacher signals to student capacity, combines distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), and applies explicit mitigations for fairness, privacy, and distributional shift. The approach is powerful but context-dependent: success depends on teacher quality, student architecture and capacity, available data or synthesis mechanisms, and careful objective and curriculum design.

papers_seen.author: Romero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthetic Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—matching teacher logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Practical deployment commonly integrates KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Key challenges include propagation of teacher errors, degradation on low-frequency or structured outputs, data and domain mismatch, privacy constraints, and heterogeneous deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for transferring predictive behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of the original performance. KD spans logits-based supervision, feature and relational matching, adversarial or synthetic data generation, and architectural or curriculum adaptations. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are aligned, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD can enable deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings and sometimes yield students that match or exceed teacher performance, but it also carries risks—propagating teacher errors and biases, struggling under data scarcity or mismatch, and requiring task-specific engineering. I argue KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines, applied conditionally with targeted remedies and validated against task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central tool to transfer performance from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones across modalities and tasks. The field encompasses diverse mechanisms — from soft-target supervision and feature imitation to contrastive and adversarial schemes — and integrates with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work highlights when and why different formulations help, how to handle limited or absent teacher data, and which practical choices matter for robustness, fairness, and domain-specific demands.

papers_seen.author: Knight
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical paradigm for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, or privacy-preserving protocols), KD routinely yields strong empirical gains across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings. However, KD is not a one‑size‑fits‑all remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, the choice of distillation signals, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate propagated errors, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns. I argue KD should be used as a task‑aware toolbox—selected and tuned to task, data, and deployment constraints—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Lynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Component for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal settings when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student design are selected for the deployment context. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all cure: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as propagated bias, poor low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically proven family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD spans outputs-only approaches (soft targets) to rich objectives that match intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, or contrastive signals. It operates across many data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free, synthetic-data), and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to achieve deployment constraints on latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity. The effectiveness of KD is strongly context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies (including augmentation, curriculum, and synthetic generation). Common failure modes include propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors, and optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, motivating targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. The methods span output-level soft-targets, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and application-specific protocols such as online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data-free approaches. KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, memory, and deployment barriers, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit protections against transferred biases and degraded rare-output behavior. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and task-aware training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Molina
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models to achieve substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of task performance. KD methods have diversified from classical logits-matching to include feature and attention matching, relational and many-to-many layer mappings, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and task- or data-aware adaptations. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, retrieval, and multimodal tasks, KD is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Although KD often yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on the choice and quality of teacher(s), the distilled signals, available data and augmentation strategy, and careful alignment between teacher and student; open challenges remain in robustness, distribution shift, low-data or data-free settings, and avoiding propagation of teacher errors.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their performance. KD has been extended from soft-label/logit transfer to a rich set of representation- and task-level objectives (feature matching, attention and relation alignment, projector modules, online/multi-teacher schemes, and data-free methods). When applied with task awareness — choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and hardware constraints — KD consistently enables substantial reductions in size and latency with modest accuracy loss. However, KD is not a panacea: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and low-frequency behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, and hardware-aware design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. The literature frames KD as a configurable toolkit that includes matching teacher outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- and relational-level transfer, adversarial or data‑free synthesis of training signals, and diverse protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, federated). KD is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical studies show distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, and other modalities, but effectiveness depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a central, task‑aware component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all cure.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Montoya

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact student models from larger teachers. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data regime, and the choice of distilled signals. The recommended position is to adopt KD as the default first-line compression strategy but to embed it in an integrated, task-aware pipeline that combines complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), data strategies (including data-free or synthetic data when needed), projector and layer-mapping designs, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger or multi-modal models to smaller or specialized models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment in constrained environments, and improve robustness or fairness. Across computer vision, natural language processing, speech, recommender systems, graph learning, generative modelling, and multimodal tasks, a broad set of mechanisms—soft-label supervision, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and ensemble methods, online/peer-distillation, and task- or domain-specific adaptations—have been developed. Empirical results demonstrate that distillation can yield compact models that approach teacher performance, accelerate training or inference, improve small-model self-supervised learning, and enable modality transfer, while theoretical and empirical analyses highlight factors that govern success: student capacity, teacher imperfection, data complexity, data augmentation, and bias-variance tradeoffs. Open challenges remain in principled theory, privacy-preserving and fairness-aware distillation, and extending distillation reliably to generative and highly structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Fernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Conditional, and Best-Practice Driven
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, the data used for distillation, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines — combining logits and feature objectives, projector modules, multi‑teacher or teacher‑adaptive designs, and data‑aware schedules — yields the most reliable results in real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated paradigm for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or composite teachers into smaller students. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD variants and protocols enable substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance when paired with task‑aware design, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. Practical deployment requires treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and addressing persistent limitations such as teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Myers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD offers a wide set of distillation signals and protocols that generalize across modalities and deployment scenarios, but its success is conditional on teacher and student design, data regime, and integration with complementary compression methods. For reliable, robust deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. KD methods include matching output distributions, aligning intermediate representations and attention, relational or contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture/behavior-aware design. Empirical evidence across modalities shows KD often recovers a substantial fraction of teacher performance and enables real-world deployment, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the data used for distillation, and strategies for mitigating transferred errors, distribution shift, privacy risks, and degraded performance on low-frequency or minority behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression: Essential but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD should be treated as the central, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines—paired with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and task‑aware engineering—because its success depends on teacher/student alignment, distilled signals, data regimes, and explicit mitigation of failure modes. KD rarely suffices on its own for reliable, deployment‑grade compression.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Extensions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core technique for producing compact, efficient models and for enabling cross-model, cross-modal, and privacy-sensitive transfer in deep learning and NLP. KD can be implemented at the logit, feature, and layer levels, and extended to ensemble teachers, data-free scenarios, federated settings, and task-adaptive architecture search. While KD often yields large efficiency gains with small accuracy loss, its effectiveness depends on data properties, teacher–student alignment, and training choices; addressing limitations such as data heterogeneity, low-frequency token degradation, and mismatched inputs requires tailored methods (e.g., feature mimicking, teacher adaptation, multi-teacher weighting, and specialized divergences). Building on empirical and methodological work across modalities, I argue that KD should be treated as a versatile, application-driven toolkit rather than a single recipe, and that future progress will come from combining representational-level distillation, teacher-aware training, and methods that reduce reliance on original training data.
