papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, multimodal, and generative settings, KD has been adapted into multiple objectives and training protocols that trade off accuracy, compute, memory, and robustness. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but reliable gains require careful design choices about transfer targets, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed as part of a task-aware compression pipeline that includes appropriate distillation targets, data strategies, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), KD can preserve most of a teacher’s performance while meeting real-world constraints on latency, memory, and privacy. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the signals and data used for transfer, and careful mitigation of transferred biases and robustness failures. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable, evidence-driven toolkit that must be tailored to specific tasks and constraints.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Collier
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Versatile, but Context-Dependent — A Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. It reliably transfers useful behavior and internal structure across vision and NLP tasks when designed with task-aware objectives, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, student capacity, and complementary compression procedures. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure.

papers_seen.author: Carter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods vary in their transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals), training protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self‑distillation), and data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free or synthetic-data). In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task-aware design choices to meet latency, memory, privacy, and robustness constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but outcomes are context dependent: success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies. Important open issues include theory for when particular signals transfer, reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, preserving long‑tail/low‑frequency behaviors, and preventing propagation of teacher errors and biases.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and deployment‑specialized models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Methods include matching soft logits, aligning intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and online protocols, and data‑aware or data‑free variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable tool within an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation, rare‑token degradation, and distribution shift. Practical deployments therefore combine careful selection of transfer targets, layer and projector design, curricula and data synthesis, and complementary compression primitives while monitoring robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data schemes, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirically, KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and objective design. Important open problems include principled theory linking transfer signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under domain shift and heterogeneous devices, and preserving rare or structured outputs in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression comprise a diverse set of techniques to produce smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring information from larger or auxiliary models. Research spans supervised teacher-student frameworks, self-distillation, multi-teacher and task-adaptive compression, and distillation combined with pruning, architecture search, adversarial training, and data augmentation. Practical work demonstrates benefits across vision, multimodal, graph, and NLP tasks, while theoretical analyses connect distillation to label smoothing, ensemble behavior, and bias–variance tradeoffs. Open challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and modalities, preserving robustness and privacy, and handling low-resource or low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD should be treated as the primary, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines: it transfers predictive behavior and internal representations, interoperates with pruning/quantization/architecture search, and adapts to data‑constrained or privacy‑sensitive regimes. However, its success is conditional on deliberate choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and safeguards for robustness and fairness; therefore KD is essential but not sufficient on its own.

papers_seen.author: Landry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Tool That Must Be Integrated for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and generative domains. Empirical evidence shows KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its effectiveness is strongly context dependent: it hinges on what signals are transferred, teacher and student capacity and alignment, availability and composition of data, and mitigation of robustness, fairness, and low‑frequency behavior issues. Therefore, KD should be treated as a first‑line, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation‑aware distillation with data strategies, projector or layer‑mapping modules, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to produce robust, deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably produces compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. KD succeeds across modalities when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student design are chosen for the target task and constraints, and its practical value is maximized when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. However, KD has concrete failure modes—teacher bias propagation, capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and degradation on rare or out-of-distribution phenomena—that require task‑aware engineering and integrated pipelines for deployment-grade results.

papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers, but it is not a standalone cure-all. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and representations across modalities when chosen and tuned with regard to teacher quality, student capacity, data regimes, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—while adopting safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Preston
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — An Argument for Integrated, Context‑Aware Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically effective and widely adopted approach for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels — logits, intermediate features, attention, relational and contrastive signals — and follow varied training protocols (offline, online/self, multi‑teacher, data‑free, and privacy‑aware). Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and generative settings show KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute; however, practical deployment requires careful matching of distilled signals to student capacity, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture design. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone solution, and I offer concrete, research‑ and practice‑informed recommendations for how to apply KD robustly in deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A rich family of techniques — soft-target/logit distillation, feature and attention matching, projector and layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and privacy-aware formulations — enable large efficiency gains while trading off fidelity, robustness, and generalization in task- and data-dependent ways. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolbox: select what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which auxiliary methods (augmentation, selective sampling, privacy mechanisms) to combine for a given deployment constraint.

papers_seen.author: Stein
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of techniques for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce latency, memory, and energy costs while preserving task performance. Across vision, language, and multimodal domains, KD has evolved beyond logits-only supervision into rich protocols that match intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized data or generator-based replay. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and careful objective and layer alignment. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, practical recommendations, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Ford
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Conditional, and Best Integrated into Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile set of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models so that compact models can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD routinely improves efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across modalities, but its practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of appropriate data, and careful mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degraded low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Therefore KD should be treated as a configurable core component of integrated compression workflows—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—rather than a turnkey, standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical, widely adopted approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), how transfers are staged (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free), and which complementary compression techniques are combined (pruning, quantization, architecture search). In practice, KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance, but it has failure modes—teacher error propagation, difficulty with low-frequency phenomena, capacity and optimization mismatch, and privacy or data-limited regimes—that require task-aware design and integration with other compression strategies. Treated as a configurable component of compression pipelines and paired with targeted remedies, KD is a practical core mechanism for deployable model compression rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Bennett
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically validated and versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely enables substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a plug‑and‑play cure: reliable compression requires task‑ and deployment‑aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. Treated as a configurable core of an integrated pipeline, KD delivers the best practical accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs for deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative, and federated settings, KD has been applied to reduce latency and memory, enable on-device or privacy-sensitive deployment, and in some cases improve robustness or calibration. The field offers a broad toolkit—logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature/attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free or generator-assisted distillation, and ensembles or self-distillation—that practitioners combine with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical success is widespread but conditional: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and nature of distillation data, and task-aware choices about what and how to transfer. Persistent challenges include teacher–student mismatch, optimization gaps, distributional shift, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, and privacy/fairness trade-offs. Current research directions emphasize joint optimization of compression primitives, federated and cross‑modal distillation, improved data-free protocols, and automated teacher–student matching.

papers_seen.author: Cardenas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central and Versatile but Insufficient Alone — Practical Position and Best Practices for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques that transfers information from larger or composite teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve generalization. KD methods span logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many teacher/student configurations. While KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, the data used for transfer, and integration with complementary compression methods; successful deployments therefore treat KD as a core component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Its practical success depends on task- and capacity-aware choice of transfer signals, careful teacher–student alignment, appropriate data strategies (including data synthesis or augmentation when original data are limited or private), and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Responsible deployment requires explicit handling of teacher quality, distribution shift, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical framework for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce computation, memory, and communication while often preserving—and sometimes improving—task performance. A broad family of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals) and protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free/zero-shot) has been developed and combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and neural architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. The effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and nature of data (real or synthetic), and design choices about what and how to transfer; common failure modes include teacher error propagation, teacher–student mismatch, optimization gaps, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolkit—selecting signals, mappings, and curricula appropriate to the task and constraints and combining KD with other compression strategies and safeguards for privacy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When used as a configurable core—selecting appropriate transfer targets, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining with complementary compression methods and data strategies—KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. Its success is context dependent: task properties, data availability, teacher quality, student capacity, privacy constraints, and deployment requirements all shape which distillation protocols and auxiliary methods will work best. Responsible application therefore treats KD as the central element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Mccall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used in Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks demonstrates that KD can produce deployable models with favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but KD alone is not a universal cure: its success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability (including data‑free synthesis), and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. For practical, robust compression, KD should be a central, configurable component of a task‑aware pipeline that incorporates complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and sample‑selection strategies, and targeted remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are no longer just ways to reduce parameter counts; when designed thoughtfully they preserve or even improve task performance, domain robustness, and privacy while enabling real-time deployment. Effective distillation requires going beyond matching output probabilities: transferring internal representations, using task- and domain-aware selection of teacher signals, leveraging ensemble or adversarial schemes when appropriate, and adopting data-aware or data-free augmentation techniques. In application domains from NLP to vision, multi-modal systems, and graph learning, tailored distillation strategies yield substantial speedups and parameter reductions with minimal loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy. This paper synthesizes evidence across diverse recent works to advocate a principled, task-centered approach to distillation and compression.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A wide variety of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational maps), protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, data-free), and integrations with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) have been developed. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive and representational information from larger or composite models into smaller, faster, or resource-constrained models. A broad set of objectives — from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level imitation, contrastive and adversarial schemes, data-free synthesis, and teacher-student co-training — have been developed and adapted to modalities and tasks in NLP, vision, graphs, retrieval, and generative modeling. Empirical work shows that combining carefully chosen distillation objectives with task-aware student design, pretraining of compact architectures, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) achieves large inference speedups and parameter reductions while preserving most teacher performance. Open challenges include data-heterogeneity and federated limits, teacher error propagation, robustness and privacy preservation, and task-specific design for structured outputs; addressing these requires principled choice of what to transfer, how to select or synthesize data, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Sensitive Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques that transfers behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and model size while often preserving most of the original performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline—choosing appropriate transfer targets, adapting objectives to student capacity and data regimes, and combining distillation with complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. However, KD is not a universal solution: capacity mismatch, teacher imperfections (including bias), data scarcity or privacy constraints, and difficulty preserving rare or structured behaviors require targeted mitigations, careful evaluation, and continued methodological and theoretical work.

Empirically, KD reduces inference latency, memory footprint, and compute while often preserving most of a teacher's task performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD methods vary in what they transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), how data are used (real, augmented, synthesized, or zero-shot), and whether distillation is performed online, with multiple teachers, or self-supervised. KD is most effective when configured to task and deployment constraints and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search). It also has well-documented failure modes—capacity mismatch, propagated teacher artifacts, degraded long-tail performance, and data-availability or privacy limits—that require explicit mitigation strategies. This synthesis summarizes established techniques, practical trade-offs, and actionable design patterns for applying KD in real-world deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure) and protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, federated) together with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search, module replacement) enable substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often retaining much of the teacher’s performance. KD’s success is context-dependent: outcomes depend on the choice of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, student capacity, data strategy, and explicit measures to mitigate bias, low-frequency degradation, and distribution shift. Treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and applying task- and data-aware design choices yields the most reliable practical results.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — A Position and Recommended Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows that KD can reduce inference cost, latency, and memory requirements and enable deployment under privacy, communication, and resource constraints. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, unbiased, or optimal compressed models: failures arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, transfer of teacher errors and biases, poor handling of low-frequency phenomena, and vulnerability under distribution shift or adversarial attack. Practical compression therefore treats KD as a core component within an integrated pipeline—combining representation-aware objectives, curriculum and sample-selection strategies, adversarial or synthetic-data generation for data-scarce regimes, and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to realize reliable, resource-aware students.

papers_seen.author: Terry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, empirically grounded toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners choose among soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or federated protocols; these methods are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Success depends on principled choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and targeted mitigations for transferred biases and distribution-shift failures.

papers_seen.author: Moss
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Core for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible set of tools for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. When designed around task goals, teacher–student alignment, and data availability, KD routinely enables large reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while preserving most of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher quality, student capacity, and data regimes, and it must be integrated with complementary compression primitives and explicit safeguards to meet robustness, fairness, privacy, and hardware constraints.

papers_seen.author: Peck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible family of methods for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks show KD can recover most of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication cost. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime and selection, the choice of transfer signals, and how KD is combined with complementary compression methods. For reliable deployment, practitioners should treat KD as a task‑aware toolbox—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student carefully, addressing data or privacy constraints, and integrating pruning/quantization or architecture-aware design—while explicitly mitigating limitations such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to compress large neural models for deployment under resource constraints and to transfer task- and domain-specific priors across models. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal problems, distillation methods go beyond matching output probabilities: modern approaches match intermediate representations, attention patterns, contrastive structure, and task-specific signals. Practical success depends on aligning teacher and student inputs and architectures, choosing losses that capture relational or localized information, addressing dataset shifts (including low-frequency token behavior), and carefully choosing which teacher signals to transfer. Several family-specific solutions (detection, retrieval, non-autoregressive translation, graph learning, vision-language, and spoken QA) show distillation can both improve accuracy and reduce inference cost, but raise challenges around data availability, heterogeneity, and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller students. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals, synthetic data) and in protocol (offline, online, self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, data-free variants). Empirical results across vision, language, generation, and graph domains demonstrate that distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is carefully designed and combined with complementary compression techniques; however, success depends on factors such as teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes including bias transfer and degraded performance on rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also uses pretraining, architecture-aware design, and safeguards for privacy and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, or specialized models. When designed around task constraints, student capacity, and available data, KD preserves much of a teacher's capabilities while enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy limits. Its greatest value comes from treating distillation as a configurable toolkit—combining soft-targets, representation matching, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and multi-teacher or self-distillation—with complementary compression techniques to meet real-world constraints. Success requires careful handling of teacher–student alignment, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias transfer, but a task-aware, hybrid pipeline makes KD one of the most practical routes to effective model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Cervantes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Essential, Powerful, but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Empirical evidence across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Successful distillation depends on deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability and preparation, and integration with complementary compression methods. Treated as a toolbox—combining soft-targets with representation matching, progressive schedules, curriculum selection, and pruning/quantization—KD is a first‑order approach for real‑world compression when practitioners explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Collier
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirically KD often recovers much of teacher performance and enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and inference cost, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and the choice of distilled signals. For robust, production-ready compression KD should be treated as a configurable core that is integrated with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data and curriculum strategies, and explicit safeguards for bias, robustness, and low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Fuller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — Toward Integrated, Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students to achieve deployable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its transfer objectives, teacher–student compatibility, and data strategy are chosen to match task constraints, but it also has well-documented failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and poor transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors). For reliable production use, KD should be treated as the configurable core of a broader compression pipeline that integrates representation-aware transfers, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, together with monitoring and mitigation for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD supports diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), adapts to data-limited and privacy‑sensitive settings, and interoperates with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its empirical strengths make KD a first‑line approach for many deployment problems, but reliable, production‑grade compression requires explicit attention to teacher–student alignment, data selection or synthesis, capacity matching, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, often ensemble or pre-trained, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD includes matching teacher outputs (soft logits), imitating intermediate representations, transferring attention or relational structures, and using multi-teacher, online, self-, or data-free protocols. In practice KD is combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. While KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve student generalization, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and match, and careful choice of distillation signals; persistent challenges include optimization gaps, distribution shift, low-frequency/rare-case degradation, bias transfer, and federated or heterogeneous-device constraints. Ongoing work focuses on principled objectives, layer-mapping strategies, privacy- and data-aware distillation, and robust, task-aware pipelines for production deployment.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Class, Task-Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable mechanism for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its objectives, data, and mappings are chosen with the target task and student capacity in mind; but KD alone does not guarantee production-ready compression. Reliable deployment requires integrating distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design), careful data and teacher selection, layer and projector design, and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and rare-behavior transfer.

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression trick into a broad set of techniques that enable efficient deployment, cross-modal transfer, federated and privacy-preserving learning, and improved generalization across domains. Empirical results across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs) show that KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining most of the teacher performance. However, the success of KD depends on careful choices — teacher quality, what to distill (outputs, features, internal representations), data availability and augmentation, and the loss or alignment mechanism — and recent work proposes multiple refinements (multi-teacher schemes, adversarial critics, projector modules, teacher-free variants) that mitigate known failure modes. The balance of empirical evidence and theoretical analyses indicates that KD is both practically indispensable for many compression tasks and a fertile area for research on how knowledge should be measured, transferred, and regularized.

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Necessity, Limits, and a Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling reduced memory, lower-latency inference, and new capabilities such as task-adaptive compression, multi-task transfer, and interpretable surrogates. At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, dataset and distribution mismatches, teacher bias transfer, and design choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relational structure) strongly affect outcomes. The most reliable results come from combining KD with complementary techniques (teacher adaptation, selective or curriculum-driven sample selection, representation matching, low-precision numerics, and scaled training procedures) and from tailoring the procedure to task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Sensitive Core of Integrated Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Treated as a configurable core of compression workflows, KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory footprint while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy are chosen to match task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not a standalone cure: reliable production deployments combine KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), targeted data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or privacy-preserving data), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagated teacher biases, and low-frequency degradation.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Benefits, Practical Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD enables deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints, and can be adapted for task-specific compression, federated and data-free settings, low-precision inference, and bias- or domain-aware transfer. However, KD also carries practical limits: optimization gaps that prevent perfect teacher matching, transfer of teacher biases, failures on low-frequency phenomena, and sensitivity to data availability and teacher-student compatibility. To realize KD's promise practitioners should choose what signals to transfer (logits, features, relations), consider multi-teacher and confidence-weighting schemes, leverage task-aware architecture search when appropriate, and adopt specialized strategies (data-free generation, reverse distillation, counterfactual augmentation, or federated protocols) to address specific failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact, deployable models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD succeeds by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations through multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational constraints) and can operate in offline, online, data‑free, and federated regimes. Its empirical strengths span vision, language, speech, multimodal, and distributed training settings. However, KD is not a standalone panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals and data strategy, and explicit steps to mitigate transferred biases, low‑frequency failures, and distribution shift. The most reliable compression outcomes treat KD as the practical core of a task‑aware pipeline that integrates representation matching, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, or architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Acosta
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques that transfer information from large teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. Methods operate at multiple levels — from soft-label/logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, and contrastive objectives — and include online, offline, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free, and adversarial synthesis protocols. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful data and training strategies; its limitations arise from teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity or distribution shift, and risks of propagating teacher errors or biases. Practical usage therefore treats KD as a configurable, task‑aware component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a single turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Spencer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Component for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, more deployable students. When treated as a configurable part of an integrated compression pipeline and tailored to task, data, and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields strong trade-offs between efficiency and task performance. However, KD has concrete limits—capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher artifacts or biases, and difficulty preserving low-frequency phenomena—that necessitate complementary methods and careful engineering. This review argues that KD should be regarded as essential but not sufficient on its own, and outlines practical recommendations and open directions for robust, context-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Thornton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD methods span soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-representation and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free protocols, and task-aware layer mapping and projector modules. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and alignment, and mitigation of transferred biases and robustness deficits.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—from logits (soft-target) transfer to intermediate-feature, attention/relational, contrastive, adversarial, multi-teacher, and data-free protocols—enable reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. Successful distillation depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data availability; practitioners generally combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training protocols. Persistent challenges include capacity and optimization mismatch, data- or privacy-constrained regimes, reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Promising directions emphasize task-aware signal selection, flexible layer mappings, multi-teacher or ensemble designs, adversarial/data-free sample synthesis, and integrated pipelines that co-design KD with other compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. Work across vision, language, graphs, and generative representations shows diverse KD objectives (soft-target, feature, relational, contrastive, and layer-matching), a range of data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free/zero-shot), and many complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, architecture search, block-structured sparsity, and cheap operators). Empirical and theoretical studies clarify when KD helps, how it interacts with data-augmentation and teacher imperfection, and how KD can be adapted for privacy-preserving or federated scenarios. This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.

papers_seen.author: Beltran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models.
