papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. A broad toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (real, synthetic, or data‑free) has been developed. KD is routinely combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and can be adapted to privacy‑sensitive or data-limited regimes. Empirically, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities, but success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and targeted mitigation for transferred errors, distribution shift, and social harms. Treating KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all recipe—yields the most reliable, deployable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing large teacher models into smaller students that can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD supports a wide range of transfer targets and training regimes and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design choices. However, KD is context-dependent: its success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of risks such as bias transfer and distribution-shift degradation.

papers_seen.author: Mccall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used in Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks demonstrates that KD can produce deployable models with favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but KD alone is not a universal cure: its success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability (including data‑free synthesis), and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. For practical, robust compression, KD should be a central, configurable component of a task‑aware pipeline that incorporates complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and sample‑selection strategies, and targeted remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lucas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically proven approach for producing compact, efficient models from large teachers. KD routinely achieves large reductions in inference cost and model size while recovering much of teacher performance, and it enables domain, modality, and privacy‑aware adaptations. However, KD is not a turnkey cure: its reliability depends on careful choices of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy, and it should be applied as the core element of a broader, deployment‑aware compression portfolio that includes pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data interventions.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. It operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals, contrastive and adversarial objectives) and is most effective when tailored to the task, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit protocols to mitigate failure modes such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and the transfer of biases or private information. Responsible application requires task-aware teacher–student design, data strategies (including data-free or few-shot methods when necessary), and monitoring for degraded behavior on low-frequency or structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Bentley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multifaceted Toolbox for Compression and Responsible Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a versatile, task- and domain-adaptive toolbox rather than a single recipe. When combined with complementary mechanisms (feature and layer matching, many-to-many alignment, data augmentation, ensembling, pruning, quantization, and privacy-preserving protocols), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving—or in some cases improving—task performance. Realizing these benefits reliably requires attention to what is distilled, how teacher and student are matched, and measures to mitigate risks such as teacher bias, data scarcity, and privacy concerns. Practical adoption should therefore treat KD as a configurable component of compression and deployment pipelines, with choices driven by the task, data availability, and safety constraints.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring behavior and representations from large teacher models to smaller student models. When applied with appropriate objectives, layer mappings, data strategies, and safeguards, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it interacts with teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, distribution shift, and fairness concerns. Treating KD as a configurable core of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum strategies, and privacy-aware protocols—yields the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A First‑Class, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (but Not a Panacea)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and highly effective approach for producing compact, efficient models across modalities and tasks. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves most teacher performance while delivering large gains in latency, memory, and deployability; however, its success depends on task-aware design choices, data availability, and careful mitigation of teacher artifacts. KD should be treated as a first‑order component of any compression pipeline and combined with complementary techniques when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Benson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Foundational, Context-Dependent Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single compression trick into a flexible framework for producing compact, deployable models and for transferring behavior across domains, modalities, and privacy-constrained settings. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods—KD enables significant reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, distillation has clear failure modes (optimization gaps, distributional mismatch, and social harms) that require targeted mitigation and careful evaluation. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, application-driven toolkit for model compression and adaptation, not a one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical set of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models in deep learning and NLP. KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends on task-aware choices: what signals to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), teacher–student alignment, available data (real, synthetic, or none), and complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Responsible and robust deployment further requires addressing distribution shift, low‑frequency or structured outputs, privacy and fairness concerns, and principled selection of distillation targets. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable toolkit — often essential for practical compression — rather than a turnkey solution; practitioners should select and combine distillation recipes according to capacity, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision and language modalities. A wide range of distillation signals (soft logits, internal features, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives), workflows (offline, online, multi-teacher, teacher‑free), and data strategies (authentic, augmented, or synthetic) have been developed and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the selection or synthesis of distillation data, and targeted mitigation of transferred biases or distribution-shift failures.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, a diverse toolbox of distillation targets, training protocols, and data strategies has been developed. Practical deployment typically treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) while attending to data regimes, teacher–student alignment, and risks such as transferred bias and degraded behavior on rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques constitute a flexible toolkit for transferring behavior and internal structure from large, high‑capacity teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment‑specific student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations, and structured objectives) and across protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co‑distillation, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free, and federated schemes). Empirical practice shows KD often retains a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in compute, memory, and latency when combined with complementary compression methods and careful data and architecture choices. However, KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: it is sensitive to teacher quality and mismatch, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and the risk of propagating teacher artifacts (biases, low‑frequency errors). Remaining needs include principled theory linking distilled signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous or non‑i.i.d. data, and robust privacy/fairness guarantees for compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Indispensable but Task‑Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD variants have been successfully adapted across modalities and tasks, and when designed with awareness of task constraints, data availability, and student capacity, distillation yields substantial practical gains. However, KD has concrete limits—capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and failures on rare phenomena—that make it most effective when integrated into broader, task‑aware compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Key
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger, often ensemble, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at the logit level, at intermediate representation and attention levels, and via relational or contrastive objectives; they are routinely combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis. Empirically, well-designed distillation pipelines can produce compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance, enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy and device constraints. Success depends on choices about what and how to transfer, the quality and alignment of teacher and student, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data; important open problems remain around distribution shift, bias/fairness transfer, low-frequency behavior, and principled theoretical understanding.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD operates via many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, adversarial or data‑free generation, and online or multi‑teacher training—and is typically combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet practical latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware design, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful engineering to avoid failure modes such as teacher error transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Terry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, empirically grounded toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners choose among soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or federated protocols; these methods are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Success depends on principled choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and targeted mitigations for transferred biases and distribution-shift failures.

papers_seen.author: Hubbard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, a diverse set of transfer targets and training protocols has emerged — from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even using synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data. Best results typically come from combining multiple distilled signals, aligning teacher and student architectures (or adding projector layers), and integrating KD with complementary compression primitives and data strategies. Despite broad empirical success, persistent challenges include handling distribution shift and low-frequency behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, safeguarding privacy and fairness, and automating principled teacher selection. This synthesis condenses prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open research directions documented in the supplied literature.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses multiple transfer signals and training protocols and is most effective when designed with task- and deployment-awareness. While KD frequently yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss, reliable deployment requires combining KD with complementary compression primitives and explicit measures to mitigate teacher imperfection, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias propagation.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Compton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Conditional Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD supports a wide range of transfer targets and training protocols, and it is most effective when treated as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data strategies. While KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, its success is context-dependent: it hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and selection, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degraded low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Realizing KD's full potential requires task-aware engineering, complementary compression primitives, and focused research on theoretical foundations and robust, privacy-preserving protocols.

papers_seen.author: Escobar
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods range from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations or using synthesized or adversarial samples; in practice KD is most effective when integrated into a broader compression pipeline and adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Distillation can transfer many types of knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive signals) and can be adapted to scenarios that lack original training data, require privacy guarantees, or demand task- and hardware-aware compression. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, architecture search, pretraining, or ensemble teaching), KD enables large reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving performance. Nevertheless, distillation can propagate biases and teacher artifacts and needs targeted remedies (feature-focused objectives, multi-teacher strategies, teacher annealing, or exposure to raw data) to avoid failure modes on rare phenomena. The literature demonstrates both the breadth of KD methods and concrete best practices to maximize effectiveness across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Stanley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. KD spans matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free protocols, and multi- or online-teacher schemes. Empirical work shows KD typically recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can interact positively with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, but its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and explicit mitigation of bias, distribution shift, and low-frequency failures. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline tailored to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Herman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Evidence, Methods, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, and multimodal tasks shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing parameters, latency, and memory. Success is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of transferred signals, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies rather than as a one-shot cure.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression: Essential but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, latency, and memory, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data regime and synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of bias, privacy, and low‑frequency failures. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with complementary techniques and deployment‑aware validation.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and widely applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD has matured into a toolbox that includes logit- and feature-level transfer, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free and adversarial generation, online and multi-teacher schemes, and task-aware layer alignment. Its effectiveness in reducing parameters, latency, and memory—often with modest performance loss—makes KD a core first-line method for deployment. At the same time, KD has clear failure modes (teacher–student mismatch, domain shift, bias transfer, limited or private data) that require task-aware protocols, complementary compression techniques, and targeted research into robustness, privacy, and automated teacher/student design.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Integrated Model Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, memory, and latency, but it is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on careful selection of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression primitives and privacy safeguards. Best practice treats KD as the configurable core of an end‑to‑end compression pipeline rather than as a standalone remedy.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teacher models. KD transfers information at multiple levels—soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational maps, and synthesized examples—and is commonly integrated with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, or privacy, but its success is conditional on task‑aware design, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as distributional shift, propagation of teacher errors, long‑tail degradation, and privacy/fairness concerns. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a universal cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Task‑aware Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across speech, vision, translation, and evaluation metrics, KD variants (soft labels, feature/attention matching, adversarial and data-free schemes, and self‑distillation) have enabled deployable models under latency, memory, privacy, and communication constraints. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with distribution or capacity mismatch, and require task‑aware adaptations. When used as part of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline—combining layer‑wise alignment, pretraining, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic data generation—KD reliably yields practical tradeoffs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: A Central but Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practically effective set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, distillation yields substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often recovering much of teacher performance. However, its success is highly context dependent: outcomes hinge on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and training protocol, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. For robust, fair, and production-ready compression, distillation should be deployed as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that combine architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, privacy, and long‑tail behavior.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression — Powerful but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, practically proven approach for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory use, and energy while preserving much of task performance. KD excels when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful teacher–student alignment, and appropriate data strategies; however, it is not a universal remedy. Reliable deployment requires treating KD as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines with explicit provisions for teacher quality, data scarcity, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely adopted set of techniques that reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Best results come when distillation is configured to the task—choosing appropriate signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity and architectures, and combining KD with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and data strategies. KD is therefore a core, configurable element of effective compression pipelines, but it is not by itself a universal cure: careful engineering and safeguards are required to address capacity mismatch, data scarcity, fairness, robustness, and preservation of rare or fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD operates at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structures—and is effective across modalities (vision, language, speech, and translation) when adapted to task constraints. KD achieves substantial reductions in latency and model size while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate transferred biases and low-frequency or out-of-distribution failures. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, central component of an integrated compression and deployment pipeline rather than as a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). A wide range of KD objectives and protocols have been developed — from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, adversarially chosen samples, and data-free or zero-shot synthesis — and these are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices, leaving open practical challenges around heterogeneous architectures, distribution shift, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A wide variety of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational maps), protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, data-free), and integrations with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) have been developed. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment in constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. The literature documents a wide set of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher–student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (data-rich, data-free, augmentation and selective-sample curricula). Empirical work across vision, language, graph, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling shows that well-designed KD pipelines — especially those that match internal representations, align layers thoughtfully, and combine KD with pruning/quantization or student-aware teacher design — can retain much of teacher performance while substantially lowering model size and latency. However, KD has failure modes (teacher mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, privacy and bias transfer, and sensitivity to data availability) that require complementary methods such as data-free synthesis, domain-aware adaptation, privacy-preserving noise, and careful objective design. The field continues to refine when and how to apply KD so that compact models are accurate, robust, and suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: The Case for Task- and Data-Aware Knowledge Distillation: Principles, Pitfalls, and Practical Extensions for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its practical success across vision, language, graph, and generative models depends not only on the generic teacher→student paradigm but on task-aware selection of transferred information, choices about data access (including data-free and privacy-preserving variants), and the use of auxiliary techniques (adversarial training, ensembling, pruning, and architecture search). When these dimensions are addressed explicitly, distillation can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while offering improved robustness, interpretability, or resource-efficiency. However, naive distillation can fail due to optimization difficulties, domain shift, and heterogeneous teacher-student mismatches, so practitioners must adopt targeted strategies that consider the learning objective, available data, and student capacity.

papers_seen.author: Jacobs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring behavior and representations from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while often preserving most of a teacher's performance. Its practical value emerges when KD is used as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines that also employ pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data strategies. At the same time, KD is not sufficient by itself: success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distillation signals, and careful handling of data, bias, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Norman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential Core but Not a Standalone Solution for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical family of techniques that transfers information from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across modalities, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression and data strategies. The recommended practice is to treat KD as a configurable, central component embedded in an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a turnkey cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Strong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and richer internal information. A broad toolbox of distillation targets and protocols has emerged—soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, self- and online-distillation, and multi-teacher schemes—and these are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD has been applied across vision, language, graphs, speech, generative models, and federated settings, yielding large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance when design choices are task- and architecture-aware. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability in optimization; practical remedies emphasize task-aware signal selection, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving protocols. This review synthesizes empirical patterns, common mechanisms, practical recommendations, and open problems for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — A Position and Recommended Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows that KD can reduce inference cost, latency, and memory requirements and enable deployment under privacy, communication, and resource constraints. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, unbiased, or optimal compressed models: failures arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, transfer of teacher errors and biases, poor handling of low-frequency phenomena, and vulnerability under distribution shift or adversarial attack. Practical compression therefore treats KD as a core component within an integrated pipeline—combining representation-aware objectives, curriculum and sample-selection strategies, adversarial or synthetic-data generation for data-scarce regimes, and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to realize reliable, resource-aware students.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from large teachers across vision, language, graph, and generative settings. KD supports deployment on constrained hardware, domain adaptation, improved interpretability, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their predictive performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-target (logit) supervision to representation- and layer-wise alignment—and integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-augmentation or curriculum strategies. Empirical evidence across vision, language, generative models, and retrieval shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher accuracy and can add benefits such as improved generalization or interpretability when applied carefully. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, optimization choices, and explicit handling of teacher biases and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component in a broader compression pipeline, chosen and tuned to the task, data availability, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Mcdaniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD is effective across modalities when treated as a configurable toolbox—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, curricula), and how to handle data constraints (augmentation, data-free synthesis, federated protocols). KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, but it is context-dependent: limitations include teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and difficulties with rare/long-tail phenomena. Best practice is to use KD as a principled component of an integrated compression pipeline, paired with task-aware design choices and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations so that compact models meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit has emerged — soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data strategies including data-free synthesis and targeted augmentation — which is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and distillation data are aligned, but KD has documented limitations (teacher–student mismatch, degradation on low-frequency behaviors, bias and privacy transfer, and sensitivity under data scarcity or distribution shift). Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals, data protocols, and complementary compression techniques according to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Little
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when it is designed as a task-aware, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression primitives; common failure modes include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher artifacts (including bias), and degraded behavior on low-frequency or shifted-distribution phenomena. Research and practice converge on the view that KD is essential but conditional: powerful when used carefully and in combination with other methods, and inadequate when applied as a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Levy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or specialized models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teachers. When integrated with complementary compression methods and task-aware engineering, KD routinely enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and objective design, and it raises open challenges in robustness, privacy, and automatic student design.

papers_seen.author: Mullins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and versatile approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical and methodological work shows KD reduces inference cost and often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities, but its reliability is conditional: success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of signals to transfer, and data availability or synthesis. Best practice treats KD not as a one-shot cure but as the central, configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline that combines distillation objectives with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data strategies to meet deployment constraints while explicitly mitigating bias, long-tail failures, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. The literature develops multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline multi-stage, online, self-distillation, data-free/generative, adversarial), and application-specific adaptations (NLP transformer compression, vision, speech, graph models, federated and privacy-aware settings). Empirical work shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, data availability, and distributional or fairness concerns. Practical success generally requires matching the distillation objective to the task, handling data limitations with augmentation or synthetic generators, and integrating KD into a broader compression portfolio (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Levy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or specialized models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teachers. When integrated with complementary compression methods and task-aware engineering, KD routinely enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and objective design, and it raises open challenges in robustness, privacy, and automatic student design.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression: Central, Configurable, and Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates at multiple levels — from soft-label/logit matching to intermediate representation and attention imitation — and is most effective when treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture design) and task-aware data strategies. Although KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance and enables deployment under resource and privacy constraints, its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and propagation of teacher biases. I argue that KD should be adopted as a primary engineering primitive for model compression, but only when combined with careful teacher–student co-design, representation-aware objectives, and complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods include transferring soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals, and can be applied in offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data-free settings. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables many practical applications across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, available data (or synthesis strategies), and careful objective design. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data strategies—and adopt safeguards for robustness, fairness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Romero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthetic Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—matching teacher logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Practical deployment commonly integrates KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Key challenges include propagation of teacher errors, degradation on low-frequency or structured outputs, data and domain mismatch, privacy constraints, and heterogeneous deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks shows KD frequently yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are carefully matched. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline alongside pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and calls for explicit strategies to mitigate teacher bias, handle data scarcity or privacy constraints, and maintain rare-token or long-tail behaviors. Remaining challenges include principled signal selection for heterogeneous architectures, robust and private distillation under non‑i.i.d. data, and automated, deployment‑aware teacher–student co‑design.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, multimodal, and generative domains show KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Practical deployment favors combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), choosing appropriate transfer targets (logits, features, attention, decision-boundary signals), and adopting data- and task-aware strategies. KD also has well-documented limitations — optimization obstacles that prevent perfect teacher matching, sensitivity to teacher quality and data regimes, and risks of propagating teacher biases or poor modeling of rare phenomena — which motivate targeted mitigations such as adversarial/sample-selection methods, multi-teacher and teacher-aware schemes, data-free or privacy-preserving formulations, and representation-level objectives. Overall, KD is best viewed as a flexible, task-aware toolkit whose effectiveness depends on matching methods and safeguards to the compression and deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Compressing Visual-linguistic Model via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite exciting progress in pre-training for visual-linguistic (VL) representations, very few aspire to a small VL model. In this paper, we study knowledge distillation (KD) to effectively compress a transformer-based large VL model into a small VL model. The major challenge arises from the inconsistent regional visual tokens extracted from different detectors of Teacher and Student, resulting in the misalignment of hidden representations and attention distributions. To address the problem, we retrain and adapt the Teacher by using the same region proposals from Student's detector while the features are from Teacher's own object detector. With aligned network inputs, the adapted Teacher is capable of transferring the knowledge through the intermediate representations. Specifically, we use the mean square error loss to mimic the attention distribution inside the transformer block and present a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align the hidden state by contrasting with negative representations stored in a sample queue. To this end, we show that our proposed distillation significantly improves the performance of small VL models on image captioning and visual question answering tasks. It reaches 120.8 in CIDEr score on COCO captioning, an improvement of 5.1 over its non-distilled counterpart; and an accuracy of 69.8 on VQA 2.0, a 0.8 gain from the baseline. Our extensive experiments and ablations confirm the effectiveness of VL distillation in both pre-training and fine-tuning stages.
