papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-capacity deep learning models in resource-constrained settings. Methods range from transferring soft labels to matching intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, synthesizing surrogate data for data-free distillation, and integrating distillation into federated and privacy-sensitive regimes. Empirical gains have been demonstrated across computer vision, generative modeling, graph learning, and natural language processing, while theoretical work and empirical studies highlight nuanced trade-offs related to regularization, sample selection, teacher quality, and heterogeneous/distributed data. Open challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher-student design, and compression of generative and transformer models for real-world low-latency deployment.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their performance. KD has been extended from soft-label/logit transfer to a rich set of representation- and task-level objectives (feature matching, attention and relation alignment, projector modules, online/multi-teacher schemes, and data-free methods). When applied with task awareness — choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and hardware constraints — KD consistently enables substantial reductions in size and latency with modest accuracy loss. However, KD is not a panacea: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and low-frequency behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, and hardware-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Sparks
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line, Task‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression (with Explicit Limits and Prescriptions)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models into deployable students because it is flexible, empirically effective across modalities, and interoperable with complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on task‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data regime, and explicit mitigations for transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and low‑frequency behaviors. Practitioners should adopt KD as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that include task adaptation, selective or curriculum distillation, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) to meet concrete deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically supported toolkit for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods often preserve most of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication cost, but their success is strongly context dependent. Reliable deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—aligned to teacher and student architectures, data availability, and deployment constraints—and combines distillation with complementary techniques and targeted safeguards to mitigate teacher error, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often retaining much of teacher performance, but its success is context dependent: it requires task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data strategies (including synthetic or privacy‑aware data), and complementary compression primitives. The most reliable deployments treat KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a stand‑alone cure, and continuing research should prioritize robustness, fairness, privacy, and principled methods for heterogeneous and low‑data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applied approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data‑free or online protocols. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks. Effective deployment treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and careful data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Drake
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile, empirically proven approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD enables substantial trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy when paired with careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle data constraints. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of propagated errors or bias. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression comprise a diverse set of techniques to produce smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring information from larger or auxiliary models. Research spans supervised teacher-student frameworks, self-distillation, multi-teacher and task-adaptive compression, and distillation combined with pruning, architecture search, adversarial training, and data augmentation. Practical work demonstrates benefits across vision, multimodal, graph, and NLP tasks, while theoretical analyses connect distillation to label smoothing, ensemble behavior, and bias–variance tradeoffs. Open challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and modalities, preserving robustness and privacy, and handling low-resource or low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Baird
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applied family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, privacy, or deployment constraints. The literature offers a broad taxonomy of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free or generative), and architecture-aware adaptations that are commonly integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across NLP, vision, visual‑linguistic models, retrieval, and specialized domains shows KD can recover much teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are addressed, but it faces recurring limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts (biases, failure modes), and challenges in reliably transferring robustness and low‑frequency behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than a single turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large, high‑capacity teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative and multimodal tasks, KD has been adapted into many targets and training regimes and is most effective when integrated with architecture‑aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the empirical strengths of KD, the principal methods and protocols, common limitations, and practical design patterns that guide successful compression and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad toolbox for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models to smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving models. Methods range from soft-logit supervision to internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence across vision, NLP, graphs, and federated settings shows KD can recover much of a teacher's performance in resource-constrained deployments, while challenges remain in teacher selection, data availability, bias propagation, and task-specific design.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. The literature frames KD as a configurable toolkit that includes matching teacher outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- and relational-level transfer, adversarial or data‑free synthesis of training signals, and diverse protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, federated). KD is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical studies show distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, and other modalities, but effectiveness depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a central, task‑aware component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all cure.

papers_seen.author: Stephens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD routinely produces compact models that retain a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success is strongly context dependent: it requires task‑aware design of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and explicit mitigations for known failure modes. The practical position argued here is that KD should be treated as the configurable, central element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis/augmentation, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student logits-matching recipe into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing models and enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware. Modern KD variants transfer not only soft labels but also internal and feature representations, employ multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, and integrate with federated and data-constrained workflows. When matched to the task (e.g., feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP, projector adapters for mismatched architectures, or privacy-aware ensembles for federated settings), KD enables small models to approximate or sometimes match larger teachers while offering routes to improved robustness and inclusivity. However, realizing these gains requires attention to teacher quality, capacity gaps, the form of distilled information, and sample-wise effects of soft targets. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable component of model-compression pipelines and present evidence-based practical recommendations for when and how to apply its variants.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Newton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD consistently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs when applied thoughtfully, but its benefits are conditional on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and architecture alignment. Best practice treats KD as the central component of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit mitigations for failure modes such as propagated bias, distribution shift, and degradation on low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Norman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential Core but Not a Standalone Solution for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical family of techniques that transfers information from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across modalities, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression and data strategies. The recommended practice is to treat KD as a configurable, central component embedded in an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a turnkey cure-all.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. A rich family of KD formulations — from logit matching and feature imitation to adversarial, data-free, and online schemes — together with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and teacher ensembles) enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while largely preserving model quality. However, KD is not universally effective out-of-the-box: its benefits and risks depend on task characteristics, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and deliberate choices of what and how to transfer. When practitioners treat KD as a toolkit of targeted strategies and validate choices against task constraints, it yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to the original model.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Tyler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster, or deployment‑specialized student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and federated settings, KD methods—including soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or data‑free generation, and self- or online‑distillation—enable substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on aligning distillation signals to student capacity and task requirements, selecting or synthesizing suitable data, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Important limitations remain (teacher–student capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, failures on low‑frequency phenomena, and distribution shift), so KD is best used as a configurable component within an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline with explicit evaluation of robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations so that compact models meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit has emerged — soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data strategies including data-free synthesis and targeted augmentation — which is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and distillation data are aligned, but KD has documented limitations (teacher–student mismatch, degradation on low-frequency behaviors, bias and privacy transfer, and sensitivity under data scarcity or distribution shift). Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals, data protocols, and complementary compression techniques according to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Davis

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical technique for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. I argue KD should be treated as a first‑class, configurable element of integrated compression pipelines rather than a one‑shot cure.

papers_seen.author: Hopkins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP

Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, data regime, teacher–student alignment, and safeguards against propagation of undesirable teacher properties; addressing open problems (robust data-free distillation, theory of transfer, fairness and privacy) requires integrating KD into end-to-end compression pipelines and co-designing students, objectives, and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically validated toolkit for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, multimodal, and other domains, KD has expanded from simple logit matching into a wide range of transfer signals, protocols, and hybrid pipelines that—when combined with careful choices about data, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression primitives—regularly recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication. Success is context dependent: reliable outcomes require attention to teacher quality, student capacity, the distillation data regime (including data-free or privacy-aware alternatives), optimization schedules, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and low‑frequency behavior. Remaining research needs include principled guidance on what and how to transfer across heterogeneous architectures, stronger theory tying distillation signals to student generalization, and robust methods for data‑scarce, privacy‑sensitive, or non‑i.i.d. settings.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, graph, and generative settings, KD techniques (logits, feature/attention matching, relational objectives, adversarial and data‑free protocols, and ensemble/online schemes) often recover a large fraction of teacher performance when paired with appropriate data strategies, pretraining, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD has concrete limits — teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, rare‑token degradation, and failures under distribution shift or scarce/private data — which motivate task‑aware design, multi‑signal objectives, and integration with other compression primitives. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, domain examples, practical guidelines, and open challenges documented in the selected literature.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an overall compression pipeline with task-aware signal selection, careful teacher–student co-design, and targeted mitigations for privacy, fairness, and domain shift.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory while retaining much of teacher performance when used with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data and complementary compression methods to apply. However, KD alone cannot guarantee reliable deployment: teacher quality, data scarcity and mismatch, capacity gaps, low-frequency phenomena, distribution shift, and bias propagation require targeted mitigations and integrated pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Gregory
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practical Considerations, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically validated family of techniques that transfers information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. KD methods include soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, many-to-many layer mappings, and data- or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when designed as a task- and deployment-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline together with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design; its empirical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis, and careful alignment between teacher and student. Remaining challenges include robustness under distribution shift, transfer of teacher biases, low-data or data-free regimes, principled layer mapping, and theoretical understanding of when and which distilled signals are most effective.

papers_seen.author: Phelps
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When applied as a configurable component of an end-to-end compression pipeline—aligned with appropriate distillation targets, data strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search—KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of the teacher performance. However, its effectiveness is conditional on factors including teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and augmentation strategy, optimization practices, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and robustness failures. Careful, task-aware design and integrated pipelines are therefore required for reliable deployment and continued research into data-free distillation, bias mitigation, and teacher–student co‑design remains crucial.

papers_seen.author: Spencer
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD operates over multiple transfer targets and training protocols, routinely improves efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression primitives and task-aware data strategies. Although KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and sometimes improve generalization or robustness, its outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability and alignment of data; consequently, KD is best treated as a configurable component of an end-to-end compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression, Robustness, and Privacy in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models. Beyond mere size reduction, contemporary KD techniques transfer internal representations, enable deployment under data- and privacy-constrained conditions, mitigate architectural and modality mismatches, and interact non-trivially with regularization practices. I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational toolchain in applied deep learning and NLP systems—one that must be combined with tailored alignment, privacy-preserving, and teacher-selection strategies to fully realize its benefits in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context‑Dependent Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically powerful approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining most of the teacher performance. Its effectiveness stems from diverse ways of transferring information (logits, intermediate features, relational structure), flexible training protocols (offline, online, self-, multi-teacher), and the ability to combine with complementary compression methods. However, KD is not a universal remedy: success depends on signal choice, data availability and quality, teacher-student pairing, and careful integration with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task‑aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Principled, Task-Aware Toolbox for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a configurable, principled toolbox rather than a single recipe. When combined with representation-level objectives, layer-mapping, data- or teacher-aware curricula, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD reliably enables practical deployment of compact models while also serving as a lever for robustness, privacy, and fairness. However, KD is not automatic: optimization gaps, teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, and low-frequency or minority behaviors limit out-of-the-box success and require targeted remedies. Practitioners should therefore select distillation signals, mapping strategies, and safeguards to align compression objectives with deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rodgers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, accurate teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target (logit) matching into a diverse toolkit (feature/attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and data-free protocols) that is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, but its effectiveness is highly context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of bias and distributional mismatch strongly influence outcomes. Practical use treats KD as a configurable core component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Sparks
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line, Task‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression (with Explicit Limits and Prescriptions)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models into deployable students because it is flexible, empirically effective across modalities, and interoperable with complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on task‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data regime, and explicit mitigations for transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and low‑frequency behaviors. Practitioners should adopt KD as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that include task adaptation, selective or curriculum distillation, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) to meet concrete deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Simmons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used Inside Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, consistently useful set of techniques for producing compact, deployable deep models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teachers into smaller students. Empirical and methodological work across vision, language, multimodal, federated, and generative settings shows KD regularly yields favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and selection, and explicit mitigation of bias, distribution shift, and rare-output degradation. For robust, production-ready compression, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation with complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and targeted safeguards for privacy, fairness, and domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for producing smaller, faster, and deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. Research has expanded KD beyond logits-only supervision into a rich set of objectives (feature and representation matching, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial/data-free schemes, and self-distillation), and into diverse data regimes from full-data to data-free, few-shot, federated, and privacy-constrained workflows. KD is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, low-precision numerics) and with teacher-aware or student-aware design choices; its empirical success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data strategies. Remaining challenges include handling architecture and distributional mismatch, avoiding propagation of teacher errors and biases (especially on low-frequency phenomena), providing privacy and robustness guarantees, and automating teacher–student co-design for task-specific outputs.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically indispensable technique for compressing and adapting large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD is highly versatile—supporting logits-, feature-, attention- and relation-level transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows—but it is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, data availability and distribution, and careful training protocol design. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines and combining it with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, data augmentation, and curriculum strategies) leads to the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Weber
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile strategy for producing compact models from larger teachers, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its empirical success across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks is well documented, but real-world gains require matching distillation signals and procedures to task constraints and student capacity and integrating KD with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for moving state-of-the-art deep models from research to real-world deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, representations, or relational structure from larger or specialized teachers to smaller students, KD enables faster inference, smaller footprints, better generalization across domains, privacy-preserving sharing, and adaptation to heterogeneous hardware and data constraints. Realizing these benefits in practice requires combining algorithmic advances (multi-teacher regimes, curriculum and projector design, augmentation and adversarial synthesis), systems thinking (federated and client-inclusive protocols), and attention to pitfalls (mismatched objectives, erased class relations). Together, the literature shows KD is not a niche trick but a broad, flexible toolkit for addressing latency, capacity, distribution shift, privacy, and interpretability in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, speech, and graph tasks, KD uses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline multi‑teacher, online/self‑distillation, data‑free or generator‑based synthesis, and federated/zero‑shot transfer). KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search or NAS) and when adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints. However, practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, low‑frequency failures, and distribution shift. Treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—choosing appropriate signals, layer mappings, data strategies, and complementary techniques—yields the most reliable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Kramer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best-Practice Driven for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teachers. KD reduces inference cost, memory, and latency and can preserve much of teacher performance across modalities. Its effectiveness, however, is conditional: success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment and capacity, data availability (or synthesis), and integration with complementary compression methods and safeguards. Treating KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with task‑aware selection of distillation objectives, data strategies, and architecture-aware transformations—yields the most reliable outcomes in real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Richard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation is Central but Insufficient: A Position on Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, latency, and memory, but reliable deployment requires integrating KD into a broader, task- and hardware-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Ponce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models across vision, language, speech, and other modalities. KD methods operate over multiple signals and protocols and are most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that also addresses data, architecture, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used in Hybrid Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically proven technique for converting large teacher models into smaller, efficient students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD reliably reduces latency, memory, and energy costs and can transfer robustness or domain knowledge, but it is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher and student design, data regime, and deployment constraints. For robust, deployable compression, KD is best treated as a configurable core component within integrated pipelines that combine representation-aware objectives, data strategies, and complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Carson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods are diverse—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—and are most effective when integrated with complementary compression tools and deployment-aware data and optimization strategies. Empirical work shows KD routinely delivers substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but important limitations remain around teacher imperfection, teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, privacy, and reliable preservation of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practically driven family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods encompass matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations and attention, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and relying on data-aware or data-free training protocols. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, and data or data-synthesis strategies. Practical application treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers information at multiple levels—soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational structure, or synthesized examples—and can be organized in diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free regimes). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design, KD routinely produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. However, KD’s success is strongly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and calibration, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and match of distillation data (or quality of synthetic surrogates), and careful objective and pipeline design to avoid propagating teacher errors or degrading long‑tail behaviour. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline, not a universal panacea.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best-Practice‑Driven for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. KD provides a flexible family of mechanisms (soft-targets, feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free or federated protocols) that, when combined with complementary compression primitives and task-aware design, yield strong empirical trade-offs between efficiency and performance. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Romero
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The field encompasses a variety of distillation targets (soft logits, internal features, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals), protocols (offline teacher supervision, online/mutual teaching, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher ensembles), and auxiliary mechanisms (data‑free synthesis, projector layers, many‑to‑many layer mapping). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and graph domains shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and architecture alignment are carefully addressed. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and when designers attend to failure modes including teacher error propagation, degraded rare‑token behavior, distributional mismatch, and fairness or privacy risks. Open directions include principled theory for when particular signals help, robust distillation under data scarcity or heterogeneous deployments, and reliable extensions to generative and structured‑prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Weber
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocols such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free or privacy-aware variants. Distillation is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data strategies; its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and loss of rare behaviors. Remaining research directions include principled theory linking distillation objectives to generalization, reliable distillation under data scarcity and heterogeneous architectures, and methods that preserve robustness, fairness, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger or ensemble teachers. It supports a wide range of objectives—logit-level transfer, feature- and representation-level matching, relational and adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings—and is applicable across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models) and settings (offline, online, data-free, federated, multi-teacher). When combined with careful teacher-student co-design, targeted data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while also serving secondary goals such as interpretability or robustness. KD is powerful but not automatic: success depends on matching objectives to tasks, mitigating teacher-induced errors or biases, and addressing optimization and data-distribution challenges.

papers_seen.author: Dunn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. By transferring predictive behavior or internal representations, KD enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training, KD forms an essential, configurable component of modern compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, multimodal and reinforcement settings, KD variants (soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives) and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, neural architecture search, data synthesis) enable practical deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover most teacher performance and, in some settings, exceed it, but success depends on data availability, teacher–student alignment, choice of distillation targets, and targeted engineering such as projectors, pre-training for compact architectures, and curriculum or multi-teacher schemes.

papers_seen.author: Durham

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically indispensable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count. Its effectiveness depends on deliberate choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student design and capacity alignment, data availability and selection, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe, KD delivers the most reliable and deployable gains.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically effective approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving most of a teacher's performance—but it is context dependent, requiring careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and deployment constraints. Treated as the configurable core of a compression pipeline and combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware data strategies), KD enables deployable models for latency- and resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings; however, practitioners must explicitly address failure modes such as capacity mismatch, domain shift, low-frequency errors, and propagated biases.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Responsible NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into efficient students while also serving as a lever for regularization, robustness, privacy, fairness, interpretability, and continual/multi-task learning. When applied thoughtfully—combining soft-label distillation with feature- and representation-level matching, layer mapping, attention or projector modules, and task-aware curricula—KD can produce lightweight models that approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance on constrained devices and specialized tasks. However, KD is not automatic: optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and mismatches in the information transferred (e.g., for low-frequency tokens or internal features) limit its effectiveness unless complemented by targeted methodological choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe: choose distillation targets (outputs, features, internal representations), mapping strategies (many-to-many layer mapping, attention, projectors), and auxiliary safeguards (privacy-preserving noise, fairness interventions, adversarial distillation) to align compression goals with safety and utility requirements.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Work across vision, generative modeling, reinforcement learning, recommendation, and language has developed diverse objectives and mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, adversarial synthesis of training data, multi-teacher/ensemble supervision, layer-wise and task-adaptive compression, and data-augmentation-enhanced distillation. These approaches trade off accuracy, inference cost, and robustness and address practical constraints such as lack of access to original training data, domain shift, fairness, and heterogeneous model architectures. Empirical results show distilled students can approach or sometimes match teacher performance while substantially reducing FLOPs, parameters, or latency, but limitations remain in data heterogeneity, low-frequency token transfer, and privacy-constrained settings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, applications, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.
