papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Thomas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, retrieval, and generative settings, KD variants—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate features or attention, relational and contrastive objectives, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis—enable substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance when designed with task-aware objectives and appropriate data strategies. Practical deployment treats KD as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines that also leverage pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data augmentation; remaining challenges include teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity and privacy constraints, low-frequency/long-tail phenomena, and principled layer alignment across heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, pragmatic framework for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teachers into compact students. KD methods span soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and variants for online, multi-teacher, data‑free, federated, and self‑distillation regimes. The most reliable deployments treat KD not as a single recipe but as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses logits-based supervision, feature- and representation-level matching, attention- and channel-wise transfers, and data-aware or data-free extensions. It is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and when practitioners adapt objectives, data strategies, and optimization schedules to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints. KD is therefore a first-line instrument for model compression, but its reliable use requires explicit, task-aware protocols that mitigate teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and transfer of undesirable teacher traits.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single recipe but as a versatile, task-aware toolkit that enables compact, efficient, and deployable models across modalities. KD methods—ranging from logit-based soft targets to feature-, layer-, and relation-level matching, and including self-, multi-teacher, data-free, and online variants—consistently trade small accuracy loss for large gains in latency, memory, and privacy. Reliable application requires careful attention to teacher quality and compatibility, what to transfer, the data regime, and interactions with regularizers and complementary compression methods. When designed around deployment constraints and task objectives, KD delivers practical, often substantial improvements for on-device inference, domain adaptation, federated settings, and robustness-sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression

KD reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves most of a teacher's performance, but its success depends on aligning distillation objectives, data, and teacher–student capacity with task and deployment constraints. Treating KD as a configurable element within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with representation alignment, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture-aware design—yields the most reliable and deployable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Francis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques constitute a practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. The field has expanded beyond simple logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free generation, curriculum and online protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when student capacity, data availability, and teacher–student alignment are appropriately managed, but important challenges remain including handling low-frequency phenomena, teacher bias propagation, distributional mismatch, and reliable transfer under data scarcity or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Mckinney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Task‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded approach for producing compact models from larger teachers to meet latency, memory, energy, and privacy constraints. KD methods span outputs-level supervision, intermediate-representation matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free synthesis, and multi- or self-distillation protocols. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with careful design about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. Nevertheless, KD is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis ability, and explicit mitigations for robustness, fairness, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines rather than a one-shot solution.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a practical, flexible approach to compressing large neural models into resource-efficient students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks — from language and retrieval to vision, generation, and graph learning — distillation techniques enable trade-offs between accuracy, compute, and memory that make deployment feasible on constrained hardware. However, the effectiveness of distillation depends strongly on the distillation objective, the information transferred (probabilities, internal representations, or structured signals), availability of original data, and care to avoid transferring undesirable teacher properties. When combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, architecture search, low-precision training, or curriculum strategies), distillation can yield compact models that approach or sometimes even exceed teacher performance while meeting practical latency and size constraints.

papers_seen.author: Knight
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical paradigm for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, or privacy-preserving protocols), KD routinely yields strong empirical gains across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings. However, KD is not a one‑size‑fits‑all remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, the choice of distillation signals, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate propagated errors, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns. I argue KD should be used as a task‑aware toolbox—selected and tuned to task, data, and deployment constraints—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behaviors and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, graph, and federated settings, KD variants—ranging from logit-based soft-label transfer to feature- and layer-level matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and ensemble or multi-teacher approaches—have enabled deployment on constrained devices, improved inference latency, and supported privacy- and domain-aware workflows. Practical deployment mixes KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-conditioning strategies; however, limitations remain around teacher–student mismatches, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data availability, and optimization stability. The literature proposes targeted remedies (attention-based layer mapping, student-friendly teacher training, few-shot and zero-shot approaches, and federated KD protocols) and points toward continued work on principled teacher design, privacy guarantees, hardware-aware objectives, and robust distillation for low-resource regimes.

papers_seen.author: Payne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, empirically validated approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task- and deployment-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline—and combined with complementary techniques and explicit safeguards—KD routinely delivers strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not automatic: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and mitigation of robustness and fairness risks.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Tool for Compression, Adaptation, Privacy, and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single compression recipe: it is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from one set of models to another. KD enables production of compact, fast models that retain much of a larger model's performance, and it can be adapted to address domain shift, limited or private data, modality-specific constraints, and even fairness or robustness objectives. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of model deployment pipelines across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and sequential tasks) and that careful selection among KD variants (logit, feature, ensemble, online, adversarial, data-free, teacher-free, and task-aware distillation) lets practitioners balance accuracy, latency, privacy, and fairness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online/co-distillation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search — and these techniques are applied across vision, language, generative models, speech, graphs, and retrieval. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance when protocols, student capacity, and data strategies are chosen thoughtfully, but success is context-dependent and important open problems remain around theory, fairness/privacy, heterogeneous or federated settings, and robust distillation for generative and structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Cisneros
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods transfer information at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention and relational structure) and succeed across modalities when integrated into task‑aware compression pipelines. While KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, reliable deployment requires explicit attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and safeguards against bias and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated paradigm for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or composite teachers into smaller students. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD variants and protocols enable substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance when paired with task‑aware design, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. Practical deployment requires treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and addressing persistent limitations such as teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance; it is most effective when combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation, and hardware-aware design). The literature also highlights several persistent challenges — teacher and capacity mismatch, optimization and data limitations, privacy and distribution shift — and converges on practical strategies such as careful choice of distillation signals, layer alignment, multi-teacher or online protocols, and synthetic-data or data-free approaches to operate under constrained access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable component of a compression pipeline and adapted to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints, KD reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on signal selection, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and integration with complementary compression methods; responsible use requires mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, low‑frequency degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Mcguire
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Component of Compression Portfolios
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces the deployment cost of large deep models while preserving much of their predictive and representational power. Rather than being a single recipe, KD is best treated as a flexible, task- and capacity-aware instrument that should be combined with complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher-induced failure modes for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically essential family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graph, generative, and multimodal tasks shows that KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameters, latency, and memory. Successful use of KD is conditional: it requires task-aware selection of transfer targets and protocols, attention to teacher–student capacity and architectural alignment, appropriate data or synthesized examples, and combination with complementary compression methods and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and long‑tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Short
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Conditional, and Integrative Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential method for producing compact models from larger teachers across modalities in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and inductive biases that yield substantial gains in latency, memory, and often accuracy. However, KD has concrete failure modes—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias transfer, and distribution shift—that limit its effectiveness when used alone. The strongest, most reliable outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable core of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that combines careful teacher engineering, targeted distillation signals, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, but its success depends on careful choices about what information is transferred, how teachers and students are aligned, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods. I argue KD should be treated as the central element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a sole solution.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Configurable, but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful paradigm for compressing large models and transferring their capabilities to smaller, deployable students. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving much of teacher performance, and its toolkit spans logits, intermediate features, attention and relational objectives, data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher schemes. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to source or synthesize data, and how to combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. When treated as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and validated against distribution shift, capacity limits, and ethical concerns, KD delivers the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Sampson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient students. KD routinely yields substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or deployment-ready compression: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, teacher–student alignment, and combination with complementary compression techniques. Treating KD as the core of a task-aware, integrated compression pipeline — rather than a one-shot solution — achieves the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. When treated as a task‑aware toolkit and embedded within an integrated compression pipeline (including pruning, quantization, and architecture design), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs across modalities. Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention, or relational signals), teacher–student alignment, data strategies (augmentation, data‑free synthesis, or adversarial sample use), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, bias transfer, and degraded treatment of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Stephenson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-side strategies (including data-free and synthesized data). Reliable compression uses KD as a configurable core within hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and task-aware data and evaluation practices.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective and versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Its practical strengths include enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints and supporting a wide range of transfer targets and training protocols. However, distillation outcomes depend strongly on task context, teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and augmentation, and explicit handling of transferred errors and biases. For reliable, production‑ready compression, knowledge distillation should be treated as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines appropriate distillation signals with complementary techniques and safeguards.

KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. A broad toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (real, synthetic, or data‑free) has been developed. KD is routinely combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and can be adapted to privacy‑sensitive or data-limited regimes. Empirically, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities, but success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and targeted mitigation for transferred errors, distribution shift, and social harms. Treating KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all recipe—yields the most reliable, deployable outcomes.

Empirical studies show distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, and other modalities, but effectiveness depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a central, task‑aware component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all cure.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted framework for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative modeling, and multimodal tasks, KD methods trade off accuracy, latency, and resource use by transferring different forms of information (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, or synthesized training examples). Empirical work shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve generalization and deployment feasibility, but KD has practical limits tied to teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, bias transfer, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment mixes careful choice of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, multi-teacher or confidence-weighting schemes, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely used framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from one or more teacher models to a student. A rich taxonomy of KD methods exists—output (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, self- and online distillation, data-free and privacy-aware schemes, and adversarial/sample-generation approaches—applied across classification, generation, translation, retrieval, graph learning, detection, and federated settings. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the form of transferred signals, the availability or synthesis of appropriate data, and choices about layer mapping and optimization. Outstanding challenges include capacity and optimization mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, limited or private data, distribution shift, and reliably distilling structured or rare outputs; promising directions emphasize task-aware signal selection, many-to-many layer mappings, adversarial/data-free synthesis, teacher-free or meta-learned schemes, and tighter integration of KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision-boundary information and combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and, in some cases, match or exceed teachers when distillation is paired with careful teacher design, layer mapping, and data or training schedules. Major limitations remain in imperfect belief matching, distribution shift, handling low-frequency phenomena, heterogeneous or privacy-constrained data, and principled teacher selection—areas where methodological and theoretical progress continues to be needed.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. When treated as a task‑aware toolkit and embedded within an integrated compression pipeline (including pruning, quantization, and architecture design), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs across modalities. Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention, or relational signals), teacher–student alignment, data strategies (augmentation, data‑free synthesis, or adversarial sample use), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, bias transfer, and degraded treatment of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Dean
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a central and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-specific tasks. KD’s flexibility—transferring soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive signals—lets practitioners tailor compression to hardware, privacy, or accuracy constraints. Empirical evidence shows that when distillation is designed task- and capacity-aware and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or progressive module replacement), students can recover much of teacher performance and gain robustness or interpretability in particular settings. At the same time, KD is not automatic: teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, teacher–student mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher errors or biases require careful protocols (sample selection, layer mapping, objective weighting, and privacy- or robustness-aware extensions). I argue KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful and broadly applicable, but demand-aware and paired with best practices to realize its potential reliably.

papers_seen.author: Bryant
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: An Indispensable but Context‑Dependent Toolbox
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When matched to task constraints, data regimes, and student capacity, KD reliably produces compact models that retain much of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections and faces limits (data mismatch, capacity gaps, low-frequency behavior), so it must be applied as a principled, task-aware set of techniques combined with complementary compression practices.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students that preserves much of teacher functionality while reducing latency, memory, and compute. KD methods span soft-logit matching, intermediate-representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD delivers substantial practical benefits across modalities and tasks when applied as part of a task-aware compression pipeline, but it is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, a diverse toolbox of distillation targets, training protocols, and data strategies has been developed. Practical deployment typically treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) while attending to data regimes, teacher–student alignment, and risks such as transferred bias and degraded behavior on rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment across domains and modalities. When designed with task-awareness (choice of distilled signal, teacher selection, and training scheme), KD can preserve accuracy while materially improving latency, memory, and privacy characteristics. Best results arise from combining multiple KD techniques (logit, feature, layer-wise, adversarial, and ensemble-based) chosen to match the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Weiss
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical, flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. The literature shows a broad family of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations), multiple training paradigms (offline, online, co-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and frequent combination with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD works both as a method for transferring predictive behavior and as an implicit regularizer, but its empirical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability (including synthesized or data‑free regimes), and careful engineering choices to mitigate optimization gaps, distributional mismatch, and transferred biases.

papers_seen.author: Singleton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows KD methods often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. However, KD exhibits well-documented failure modes—capacity and architecture mismatch, transfer of teacher errors and biases, degraded long-tail behavior, and sensitivity to data regimes—that require complementary algorithmic and pipeline-level remedies. Treating KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression strategy (combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and careful data or privacy protocols) is the most reliable path to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. It supports multiple information-transfer mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and can be adapted to constrained settings (limited data, privacy, heterogeneous devices). KD is most effective when used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or pretraining—and when practitioners mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, or teacher–student mismatch. With careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers, which data to use), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving task performance across modalities.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes the state of knowledge distillation (KD) as a core set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. It surveys common distillation targets and protocols, empirical patterns of when KD succeeds or fails, practical integrations with other compression primitives, and recurring open challenges. The goal is to provide practitioners and researchers with a concise, evidence-based view of what KD reliably achieves and which design choices matter most for deployable model compression.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. When combined with pre-training, careful choice of distillation signals, data- and task-aware strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture replacement), KD produces compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, availability or synthesis of data, alignment of internal representations, and consideration of fairness and robustness. Best practice therefore treats KD as a flexible toolkit—mixing soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-level matching, online/ensemble schemes, and domain-aware adjustments—to meet practical production requirements.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while preserving task performance. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and in multiple training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, recommender, and generative settings shows KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains when combined with task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning and quantization. However, KD is context dependent: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and mitigation of failure modes including propagation of teacher errors, degraded long‑tail behavior, and privacy risks. Treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, and combining it with tailored safeguards and auxiliary methods, is the prevailing practical recommendation.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students) to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on constrained devices, and support privacy- or resource-constrained settings. Approaches span soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, data-free and zero-shot methods, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, task- and modality-specific objectives, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D detection, recommender systems, and multiple NLP tasks demonstrates that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while significantly reducing latency and memory. The literature also provides growing theoretical insight into when and how distillation helps, and identifies open challenges including imperfect teachers, domain shift, low-frequency token fidelity, modality mismatch, and heterogeneous-device federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Johnston
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and broadly useful approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods span soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free schemes, and variants such as multi‑teacher, online, and self‑distillation. KD routinely yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and performance when it is designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and task constraints, and when it is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). However, KD is not a universal recipe: practical success requires task‑aware choices, careful layer or feature alignment, and explicit remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and transferred biases. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable component within compression pipelines and offers evidence‑based best practices and caveats for its effective use.

papers_seen.author: Flores
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Findings and Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and generative tasks, KD has been adapted to many transfer targets and training protocols and is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives and task-aware design. While KD routinely reduces inference cost and preserves much of teacher performance, it has concrete failure modes—capacity and optimization mismatch, teacher error/bias transfer, data scarcity, and difficulties preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors—that require targeted remedies and integrated compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Vang
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets and training protocols and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods to meet deployment constraints. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategies, and careful choice of distilled signals and training procedures.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Uses, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical deployments use KD as one component in an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—and require task‑aware choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Known limitations include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, degraded performance on long‑tail or rare outputs, and sensitivity to distribution shift; these motivate multi‑teacher, selective, or data‑synthesis protocols and careful evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Findings and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, latency, privacy, and domain constraints. Across modalities, KD variants—soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate representation and attention alignment, adversarial or data-free schemes, and online/self-distillation—routinely yield compact students that recover much of a teacher's performance when combined with careful data, optimization, and architecture choices. Practical success requires embedding KD in an integrated compression pipeline and attending to teacher/student design, data regimes, and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Cole
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default First‑Line Tool for Practical Model Compression — but Not a Standalone Solution
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. Empirical work demonstrates that KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while delivering substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory. However, KD alone does not address all deployment concerns: its success depends on teacher–student alignment, the distilled signal, data regime, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and hardware constraints. For reliable production use, KD should be treated as the default first-line compression mechanism that is deliberately configured and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and data strategies to meet task and deployment requirements.

papers_seen.author: Riggs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Context‑Dependent Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of larger teachers' performance. KD should be treated as a first‑order component of compression pipelines, but it is not sufficient on its own: reliable deployment requires task‑aware objective selection, attention to teacher–student compatibility and data regimes, and combination with complementary compression and privacy techniques.

papers_seen.author: Sparks
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line, Task‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression (with Explicit Limits and Prescriptions)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models into deployable students because it is flexible, empirically effective across modalities, and interoperable with complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on task‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data regime, and explicit mitigations for transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and low‑frequency behaviors. Practitioners should adopt KD as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that include task adaptation, selective or curriculum distillation, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) to meet concrete deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and versatile approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations via multiple signals (logits, features, attention, relational objectives) and supports a wide range of training protocols and data regimes. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on careful, task‑aware design, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and combination with complementary compression methods to mitigate capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and potential bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the Default First‑Line, Task‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When matched to student capacity, teacher quality, and the available data, and when combined with complementary compression techniques, KD routinely enables favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs for deep learning and NLP. However, KD is not a universal cure: reliable deployment requires task-aware design, explicit mitigation of failure modes (capacity mismatch, transferred biases, distribution shift, and poor long‑tail behavior), and integration into an end-to-end compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture choices, and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a first‑class, configurable component of any practical model‑compression strategy for deep learning and NLP. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations across tasks and modalities and, when combined with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies, produces favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. Its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, and data regimes; responsible deployment requires explicit mitigation of transferred biases, rare‑token failures, and distribution shift, plus task‑aware evaluation and privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies have become central to deploying large neural networks in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, multimodal, and language domains, researchers have developed approaches that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller students via logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial objectives. Work spans supervised and unsupervised settings, data-free or black-box scenarios, continual and federated use-cases, and concerns such as privacy and adversarial robustness. Practical recipes combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, progressive module replacement, and many-to-many layer mapping to balance accuracy, latency, and memory. Open challenges remain in data- and domain-limited regimes, robust and private compression, and principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer for a given downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods (logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data- or generator-based synthesis) and training regimes (offline, online, self-, and multi-teacher) are routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, available data or synthesis strategies, and mitigation of failure modes such as propagated teacher bias, optimization and capacity mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student co-design, and targeted safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick; it is a versatile, practically proven framework that enables resource-efficient deployment, privacy-preserving learning, cross-modal and cross-domain transfers, and even improvements in robustness. When combined with complementary techniques — feature mimicking, projector modules, teacher annealing, label-smoothing–style regularization, and data-free or federated protocols — distillation can address the main bottlenecks of modern deep and multilingual models: size, latency, heterogeneity of devices, limited or private data, and domain shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in any strategy for compressing or adapting deep models for real-world NLP and vision deployments.
