papers_seen.author: Richard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation is Central but Insufficient: A Position on Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, latency, and memory, but reliable deployment requires integrating KD into a broader, task- and hardware-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Watson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or composite teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. The literature shows a broad toolkit — logits/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-aware or data-free protocols — that is effective across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized tasks when matched to task, data, and student capacity. Empirical evidence consistently finds that KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable practical deployment, but success is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student architecture and capacity, the choice of transfer signals, data strategies (including selective or synthetic data), and integration with complementary compression techniques. Important open questions remain about principled theory, robust transfer under distribution shift and scarce data, preserving rare or structured outputs, and avoiding transfer of teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals), how data is used or synthesized, and whether distillation is performed offline, online, or zero-shot. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and federated settings, KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and match, and the chosen distillation objective; combining KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation) and task-aware protocols improves reliability. Remaining challenges center on theory-guided transfer choices, robust data-free distillation, mitigation of transferred biases, and automated teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Mack
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD enables meaningful reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving much of teacher performance, but its success is conditional on task- and data-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Moss
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Core for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible set of tools for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. When designed around task goals, teacher–student alignment, and data availability, KD routinely enables large reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while preserving most of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher quality, student capacity, and data regimes, and it must be integrated with complementary compression primitives and explicit safeguards to meet robustness, fairness, privacy, and hardware constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cordova
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely reduces inference cost and memory while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its reliability is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, architecture alignment, and complementary compression primitives critically shape outcomes. A pragmatic recommendation is to treat KD as the central component of compression pipelines while explicitly adapting objectives, data protocols, and auxiliary methods to the deployment constraints and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and broadly effective set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD reduces latency, memory, and communication costs while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance; its toolbox includes soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocols ranging from offline to online, multi-teacher, and data-free distillation. However, KD’s success is conditional on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to obtain or synthesize distillation data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design). Responsible, robust deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: What is known about Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression strategies form a broad, practically driven toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, graph learning, self-supervision, and reinforcement learning—research has developed many algorithmic variants (logit and feature matching, attention/relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes), system-level protocols (federated, black-box, data-free), and architecture-aware methods (task-adaptive compression, neural architecture search, pruning and quantization combinations). Empirically, KD often substantially reduces latency and parameter counts while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance, but its success depends on teacher–student alignment, available data and augmentations, and task-specific design; remaining challenges include teacher bias transfer, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, domain shift, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Practical deployments balance distilled signals, data strategies, and architecture choices to achieve required trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single trick into a broad, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-aware models while retaining much of their performance. The techniques differ by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel statistics), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, data-free/zero-shot, few-shot), and which complementary strategies are used (projectors, mixup/data augmentation, pruning, or architecture-aware design). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and as a regularizer; success depends critically on choices about teacher signals, student capacity, the availability and nature of data, and task-specific design. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or private data, preventing transfer of teacher errors, adapting to heterogeneous or federated settings, and scaling distillation to very large models and complex structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical, widely adopted approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), how transfers are staged (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free), and which complementary compression techniques are combined (pruning, quantization, architecture search). In practice, KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance, but it has failure modes—teacher error propagation, difficulty with low-frequency phenomena, capacity and optimization mismatch, and privacy or data-limited regimes—that require task-aware design and integration with other compression strategies. Treated as a configurable component of compression pipelines and paired with targeted remedies, KD is a practical core mechanism for deployable model compression rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal signals from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference latency, memory footprint, and deployment cost while often preserving much of the original performance. A broad set of objectives and protocols has been developed (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational/contrastive losses, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data‑free or privacy‑aware protocols), and KD is commonly combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success requires task‑ and deployment‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and explicit mitigations for failure modes including capacity mismatch, distribution shift, rare‑output degradation, and transferred biases.

papers_seen.author: Hayes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD has expanded beyond simple soft-target matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design) and task- and data-aware practices, KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but its success is context dependent and requires careful attention to teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically supported toolkit for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods often preserve most of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication cost, but their success is strongly context dependent. Reliable deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—aligned to teacher and student architectures, data availability, and deployment constraints—and combines distillation with complementary techniques and targeted safeguards to mitigate teacher error, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression, Robustness, and Privacy in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models. Beyond mere size reduction, contemporary KD techniques transfer internal representations, enable deployment under data- and privacy-constrained conditions, mitigate architectural and modality mismatches, and interact non-trivially with regularization practices. I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational toolchain in applied deep learning and NLP systems—one that must be combined with tailored alignment, privacy-preserving, and teacher-selection strategies to fully realize its benefits in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Conditional Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving—and sometimes improving—task performance. KD methods operate at logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision boundaries and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data- or privacy-aware procedures. KD delivers strong practical benefits across modalities and tasks but requires careful teacher–student alignment, attention to data and privacy constraints, and complementary techniques to address capacity gaps, domain shift, and rare-token behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Integrated Model Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, memory, and latency, but it is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on careful selection of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression primitives and privacy safeguards. Best practice treats KD as the configurable core of an end‑to‑end compression pipeline rather than as a standalone remedy.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative tasks. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, features, attention, or generated data), data strategy, and teacher–student alignment, KD routinely yields substantial inference and memory gains while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is bounded by data availability, teacher quality, capacity mismatch, and potential transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors, so it is best used as part of an integrated compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Empirical results across vision, language, retrieval, detection, generative models, and distributed settings show KD can close much of the performance gap between large and compact models, but best outcomes require tailoring what and how knowledge is transferred and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques and domain-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and versatile approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations via multiple signals (logits, features, attention, relational objectives) and supports a wide range of training protocols and data regimes. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on careful, task‑aware design, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and combination with complementary compression methods to mitigate capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and potential bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Barker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad and practical toolkit—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free protocols, and multi-teacher or self-distillation schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD frequently produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful design choices for distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Kline
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into compact student models. The literature provides a rich toolbox—output-level (soft targets), intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and variants such as multi-teacher, online/self-distillation, data‑free and meta‑learning approaches. Empirical and conceptual work agrees that KD is most effective when adapted to task constraints, student capacity, and data availability and when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design).

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and versatile toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A broad family of distillation objectives and protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, contrastive, adversarial, and data‑free approaches—and KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design. Success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and explicit handling of distribution shift, low-frequency behaviors, privacy, and architecture heterogeneity.

papers_seen.author: Coffey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD methods span soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational or contrastive objectives, and specialized protocols for data-free, federated, cross‑modal, and adversarial settings. KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Meza
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD has proven effective across modalities and tasks, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, objective selection, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases. For reliable, production-ready compression, KD should be used as a configurable, task-aware core within integrated pipelines that combine distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design) and careful data and evaluation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Bauer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically proven approach for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models so they meet latency, memory, compute, and deployment constraints. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness. While KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities, reliable deployment requires deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical Tool that Requires Task-Aware, Complementary Engineering
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile strategy for producing compact models from large teachers that supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD reliably reduces inference cost while often preserving most of a teacher's performance, but its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints and student capacity. Best outcomes arise when KD is treated as part of an integrated compression pipeline that includes representation alignment, data- and task-aware strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. KD encompasses many targets and protocols and—when designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data, and complementary compression methods—regularly yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: careful protocol design, combination with pruning/quantization/architecture search, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and long‑tail behaviors are required for dependable real‑world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Yet Contextual, Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has repeatedly enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost across modalities while retaining much of the performance of larger models. Empirical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, inductive biases, and task-specific capabilities from teacher to student, and can be adapted via logit-, feature-, and layer-level objectives, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial procedures, and data- or privacy-aware variants. However, KD is not a universal solution: optimization difficulties, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and propagation of teacher errors limit its effectiveness unless combined with careful protocol design and complementary compression techniques. I argue KD should be treated as a first-class tool in compression toolkits, but only when used with task-aware filtering, capacity-aware targets, and architecture- or data-aware refinements to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient students for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-/self-distillation, and data-free protocols—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks. KD is most effective when integrated into task-aware pipelines that align teacher and student architectures, choose appropriate transfer signals, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) while explicitly addressing limitations such as distribution shift, teacher-induced biases, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Hays
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, practically oriented family of methods for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has diversified beyond simple soft-target (logit) matching into a toolbox that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher training, self-distillation, data-free or zero-shot schemes, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD routinely improves student efficiency–accuracy trade-offs and supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success is highly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and selection (or synthesis) of data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, optimization mismatch, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a single plug-and-play algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from large teachers across vision, language, graph, and generative settings. KD supports deployment on constrained hardware, domain adaptation, improved interpretability, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Paul
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, KD routinely reduces inference cost and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distillation signal, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, context‑aware core within integrated compression pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and low-frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Synthesis of the Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller students. Across modalities and training protocols, distillation operates at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware design. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful objective and optimization design; important limitations include teacher error propagation, impaired modeling of low-frequency phenomena, and distribution-shift vulnerabilities.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Burgess
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods include output-level supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, online and multi-teacher protocols, and progressive or task-aware procedures. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative and multimodal tasks shows that when KD is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task- and data-aware engineering, it often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing resource cost. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Important open challenges remain in principled selection of distillation targets, reliable transfer under data scarcity and distribution shift, avoiding propagation of teacher biases and rare-token degradation, and automated, hardware-aware co-design.

papers_seen.author: Simmons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Versatile, but Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable paradigm for producing smaller, deployable models from larger teachers. KD provides many transferable signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational structure, contrastive objectives, and synthetic/data‑free protocols) and is effective across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks when paired with task- and capacity-aware design. However, KD has predictable failure modes—propagation of teacher errors and biases, capacity and distribution mismatches, difficulty preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors, and data/privacy constraints—that limit its reliability as a sole compression method. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design), explicit teacher–student alignment, targeted data or synthetic-data strategies, and evaluation/mitigation for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Evidence, Methods, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically validated set of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A broad toolkit—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis, and curriculum or adversarial sample selection—enables students to retain much of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, retrieval, and federated settings. Despite strong empirical successes, important engineering and scientific challenges remain around teacher–student alignment, data availability and synthesis, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, robustness and fairness, and principled automated design for heterogeneous deployment environments.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Jacobs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically essential family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller, deployable students. A broad toolkit of transfer targets and training protocols has been developed and routinely combined with complementary compression methods to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when applied with task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to train, and how to integrate with pruning, quantization, and architecture design; its reliability is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques transfer information from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models. The literature shows a diverse set of objectives and protocols—soft-label matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, and adversarial or generator-based sample augmentation—that together enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while trading off accuracy, robustness, and fairness. Empirical results indicate distilled students often approach teacher performance with substantially lower cost, but important limitations persist (teacher bias transfer, low-frequency token degradation, data access constraints, and capacity mismatch), motivating hybrid pipelines that combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and careful teacher–student design.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile set of methods for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD spans soft‑target/logit matching, representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and can be deployed in offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free, and privacy‑aware regimes. When combined with architecture‑aware choices and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD regularly yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, graphs, speech, and multimodal tasks. Empirical effectiveness is strong but conditional: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and selection, and objective design. Important open problems include principled theory linking transferred signals to student generalization, robust distillation under domain shift or scarce/private data, and preserving rare or structured behaviors in sequence and generative tasks.

papers_seen.author: Mann
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. The literature has expanded KD beyond simple soft-target matching to include representation- and structure-level objectives, a variety of training schedules (offline, online, self-distillation, data-free), and many task- and architecture-aware adaptations. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves most of teacher performance and sometimes improves robustness or calibration, but outcomes are sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the data available for distillation, and the particular signals chosen for transfer. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture choices—and emphasizes task-aware design, data strategies, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Fuller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — Toward Integrated, Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students to achieve deployable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its transfer objectives, teacher–student compatibility, and data strategy are chosen to match task constraints, but it also has well-documented failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and poor transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors). For reliable production use, KD should be treated as the configurable core of a broader compression pipeline that integrates representation-aware transfers, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, together with monitoring and mitigation for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when objectives, teacher–student alignment, and data strategies are chosen to match task and deployment requirements. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degradation on low‑frequency or out‑of‑distribution phenomena, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representational, output‑level, and data-side interventions with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Coleman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficiently Complete Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical set of techniques that enables production of compact models that retain much of larger teachers' functionality across modalities and tasks. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component of a broader compression pipeline, KD supports deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and hardware constraints. However, distillation has concrete failure modes — propagation of teacher errors, difficulty preserving low-frequency phenomena, capacity and distribution mismatches, and privacy or robustness concerns — which require complementary methods, data strategies, and careful teacher–student design. I argue KD should be adopted as a central, configurable tool in compression workflows but not relied on alone: best practice integrates KD with representation-aware objectives, curriculum/data strategies, multi-teacher or collaborative teaching, and targeted safeguards for bias, rare-case behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary approaches for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans methods that transfer soft-labels, internal feature representations, and ensemble knowledge; extensions address teacher imperfections, data scarcity or privacy, task-specific adaptations for NLP and vision, and hardware-aware compression. Empirical work demonstrates that careful design choices—such as which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student layers, whether to incorporate self-distillation or multi-teacher training, and how to combine pruning or low-precision numerics—substantially affect final accuracy and efficiency. The field also benefits from theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Remaining challenges include distilling robust semantics for low-frequency phenomena, distillation without access to original data, and co-design for hardware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective technique for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal settings. KD reliably improves student performance when matched to task constraints, but it is not a standalone solution: best outcomes arise when distillation is integrated with complementary compression primitives, careful data strategies, and explicit safeguards for privacy and fairness. Treating KD as a configurable core of compression pipelines—rather than a one-size-fits-all cure—enables more reliable, robust, and deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limitations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible method for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more interpretable models across vision, language, speech, and recommendation systems. KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal structure from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods include output-level soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online/self- and multi-teacher protocols, and data‑free or privacy-aware synthesis. When combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design, KD routinely produces substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter footprint while retaining much of teacher performance. The effectiveness of KD is highly context dependent: it relies on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis strategies, and explicit treatment of robustness, fairness, and privacy. Remaining challenges include principled teacher–student design, reliable distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, mitigation of bias transfer, and automation of distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Dependent, Foundational Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses many mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, data‑free and multi‑teacher schemes) and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, curriculum, domain adaptation). Its power for deployment in resource‑ or privacy‑constrained settings is well documented; however, KD is not universally sufficient. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher‑student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, bias transfer, and degradation on rare phenomena. The pragmatic stance advocated here is to treat KD as a configurable component of a broader compression and deployment pipeline, tuned to task, data regime, and safety constraints.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory and compute while preserving much of task performance. KD techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and contrastive signals, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data-free or domain-adaptive variants. Empirical evidence shows KD is a practical first-line strategy for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but it is not a standalone cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, objective design, and careful integration with complementary compression tools. For robust, real-world deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with targeted engineering to mitigate failure modes such as capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and distribution shift.
