papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, and privacy. The literature develops a broad taxonomy of distillation signals (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention and relational maps, contrastive objectives), training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free and federated), and integrations with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows distilled students can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while greatly improving efficiency, but success is context-dependent, hinging on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of bias, robustness, and privacy risks. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component within integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone recipe, and open problems remain in principled choice of distilled targets, reliable distillation with limited or private data, and theory connecting distilled signals to student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically grounded family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and deployment-ready models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into compact students. KD techniques include soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and adversarial- or sample-based refinements. KD interoperates with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and supports diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, multi- and ensemble teachers, online/self-distillation, data‑free and privacy-aware regimes). Practical success routinely requires task- and deployment-aware choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, rare-output degradation, and transferred biases. Key open directions include principled theory for when particular signals transfer well, robust and private distillation under limited or heterogeneous data, and reliable distillation across heterogeneous architectures and structured/generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Responsible NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into efficient students while also serving as a lever for regularization, robustness, privacy, fairness, interpretability, and continual/multi-task learning. When applied thoughtfully—combining soft-label distillation with feature- and representation-level matching, layer mapping, attention or projector modules, and task-aware curricula—KD can produce lightweight models that approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance on constrained devices and specialized tasks. However, KD is not automatic: optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and mismatches in the information transferred (e.g., for low-frequency tokens or internal features) limit its effectiveness unless complemented by targeted methodological choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe: choose distillation targets (outputs, features, internal representations), mapping strategies (many-to-many layer mapping, attention, projectors), and auxiliary safeguards (privacy-preserving noise, fairness interventions, adversarial distillation) to align compression goals with safety and utility requirements.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Duran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression — Powerful but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, practically proven approach for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory use, and energy while preserving much of task performance. KD excels when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful teacher–student alignment, and appropriate data strategies; however, it is not a universal remedy. Reliable deployment requires treating KD as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines with explicit provisions for teacher quality, data scarcity, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile toolkit for producing compact models from larger teachers. When designed and validated against task and deployment constraints, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute; however, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data strategy, and complementary compression and safeguarding measures.

papers_seen.author: Morton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, flexible paradigm for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so they can be deployed under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. When designed with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search), distillation routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance. However, distillation is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the distillation signals chosen; it can propagate teacher artifacts and struggles with optimization gaps, capacity mismatch, and low-frequency behavior. Addressing these limits requires joint teacher–student design, confidence- or curriculum-aware sample selection, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis when data are unavailable, and incorporation into broader compression pipelines tailored to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied set of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teacher ensembles or single models. The literature shows a rich taxonomy of distillation signals (soft logits, feature- and attention-level targets, relational/contrastive objectives), protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self- or co-distillation), and engineering integrations (projector adapters, curriculum or confidence-weighting, data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and cross-modal tasks indicates that carefully designed KD pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost; however, practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and mitigating failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded rare-output behavior, and capacity mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Carson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods are diverse—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—and are most effective when integrated with complementary compression tools and deployment-aware data and optimization strategies. Empirical work shows KD routinely delivers substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but important limitations remain around teacher imperfection, teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, privacy, and reliable preservation of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Stephens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD routinely produces compact models that retain a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success is strongly context dependent: it requires task‑aware design of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and explicit mitigations for known failure modes. The practical position argued here is that KD should be treated as the configurable, central element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis/augmentation, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical toolkit for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. A rich family of distillation targets and protocols has been developed (from soft logits to feature- and relation-based objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data- or privacy-aware variants), and KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods and task-aware data and architecture strategies. Success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and augmentation, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and degraded behavior on rare or out-of-distribution phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Carter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods vary in their transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals), training protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self‑distillation), and data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free or synthetic-data). In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task-aware design choices to meet latency, memory, privacy, and robustness constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but outcomes are context dependent: success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies. Important open issues include theory for when particular signals transfer, reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, preserving long‑tail/low‑frequency behaviors, and preventing propagation of teacher errors and biases.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Configurable Core of Practical Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated toolkit for compressing large models into compact, deployable students. KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication cost, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression primitives. Treating KD as a configurable core element of an end‑to‑end compression pipeline — with targeted choices about what to transfer, how to map layers, how to handle scarce or private data, and how to mitigate transferred errors and biases — yields the most reliable, deployment‑ready compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Gillespie
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target (logit) matching into a diverse toolbox that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher training, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows that KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while delivering latency, memory, and deployment benefits, but its success is context dependent: it requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, data strategy (including synthetic or privacy-preserving data), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, optimization mismatch, and degradation on rare or low-frequency phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core element within hybrid compression pipelines rather than as a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Harrison
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single teacher-to-student logits-matching recipe into a large, task-aware toolbox for producing compact, efficient models in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Research documents many variants (soft logits, feature and relational matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, data-free and privacy-aware procedures, multi-teacher and online schemes) and shows that KD, when combined with complementary compression methods and task-specific design choices, can deliver substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining most of a teacher's performance. Effectiveness depends on teacher quality, choice of transfer signals, availability and manipulation of data, student capacity, and deployment constraints; important open problems include theoretical guarantees, optimization gaps, distribution shift, privacy, and preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Rose
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across vision and NLP, KD methods include soft-target/logit supervision, imitation of intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, and data‑free or generator-based synthesis; they are used in offline, online, and self-distillation protocols and are most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers most of a teacher's performance while reducing latency, memory, and energy costs, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distillation signals, and data availability. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Maynard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and deployment complexity. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful choice of distillation signals. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, task-aware core of integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-level objectives, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to meet practical deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across modalities and tasks KD enables major reductions in inference cost and model size while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. The family of approaches includes logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and multi-teacher or self-distillation workflows. Effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and preparation, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods. Common application areas include classification, sequence modeling, generation, multimodal transfer, and domain adaptation; persistent challenges include capacity mismatches, propagation of teacher errors or biases, preserving rare or long-tail behavior, and privacy-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Burke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving or sometimes improving task performance. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component and combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, layer mapping, or data synthesis), KD yields favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across modalities and supports deployment under latency, privacy, and data-constraint requirements. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, how layers are aligned, and which training data or augmentations are used.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for transferring behaviors and representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while preserving much of task performance. KD variants operate on soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure, and can run in offline, online, data‑free, or federated regimes. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often recovers most of a teacher’s accuracy and can improve student generalization or robustness when combined with complementary compression methods (quantization, pruning, architecture adaptation) and careful data and training strategies. However, KD is context sensitive: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, selection of distilled signals and layer mappings, availability and curation of data (or synthetic alternatives), and mitigation of failure modes like teacher bias, capacity mismatch, and degraded long‑tail behavior. Treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and applying targeted remedies (selective sample choices, projectors, teacher annealing, multi‑signal objectives) produces the most reliable practical results.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide flexible, broadly applicable ways to transfer performance from large teacher models to compact student models so they can run under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. A diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel maps, relational signals) and procedures (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, meta-learned teachers, data-free synthesis) have been developed and integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, ensembling). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and recommendation systems shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve deployability, though success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Remaining directions include automated, task-adaptive transfer choices, robust data-free distillation, and principled controls for fairness and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Ware
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Insufficient Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices, supports privacy-aware and data-limited settings, and generalizes across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models). However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on the choice of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and complementary engineering (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and training pipelines). Reliable, high-quality compression therefore treats distillation as a core technique within a broader, task-aware compression strategy rather than as a standalone solution.

Best practice treats KD as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation signals, data strategies, and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Carson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods are diverse—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—and are most effective when integrated with complementary compression tools and deployment-aware data and optimization strategies. Empirical work shows KD routinely delivers substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but important limitations remain around teacher imperfection, teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, privacy, and reliable preservation of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Gillespie
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target (logit) matching into a diverse toolbox that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher training, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows that KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while delivering latency, memory, and deployment benefits, but its success is context dependent: it requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, data strategy (including synthetic or privacy-preserving data), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, optimization mismatch, and degradation on rare or low-frequency phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core element within hybrid compression pipelines rather than as a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Rose
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. KD encompasses many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free and privacy-aware variants). Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines appropriate distillation objectives with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies) and careful evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large models and transferring knowledge across architectures, datasets, and modalities. Research has advanced along several axes: designing distillation objectives (logit- and feature-based), aligning intermediate representations, performing distillation without access to original data, applying KD for domain adaptation and continual learning, and compressing or distilling generative and multimodal models. Practical deployments emphasize heterogeneous teacher-student settings, privacy and federated scenarios, and task-adaptive compression for resource-constrained inference. This review synthesizes the main methods, empirical findings, and practical considerations reported across recent work, and highlights open challenges and promising directions.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Patterns, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically essential family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information beyond hard labels. Research across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and reinforcement-learning settings has produced a toolkit of transfer targets and training protocols that, when combined with complementary compression primitives, routinely yield large reductions in latency and memory with modest performance loss. KD’s success is highly context-dependent: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and careful objective and curriculum design. Remaining challenges include robustness under distribution shift, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, bias transfer, and privacy-aware or data-free regimes; best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all remedy.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized student models. KD techniques include soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free protocols, and variants for online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and few‑shot regimes. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, and privacy. However, KD’s success is context dependent: it requires careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, distilled signals, data strategy (including synthetic or privacy-aware data), and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Reliable application therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, with explicit measures to mitigate failure modes like bias transfer, degraded long‑tail performance, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models using targets ranging from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals. Across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation or synthetic-data generation) enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical results show distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can sometimes match or exceed teachers when distillation is carefully designed. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity mismatch, optimization and belief-matching limits, distribution shift and domain adaptation, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, and avoiding transfer of teacher biases. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, practical variants, representative empirical patterns, and recommended directions for research and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable mechanism for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its objectives, data, and mappings are chosen with the target task and student capacity in mind; but KD alone does not guarantee production-ready compression. Reliable deployment requires integrating distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design), careful data and teacher selection, layer and projector design, and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and rare-behavior transfer.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or specialized models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble and multi-teacher schemes, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and layer-mapping strategies — and these methods are combined routinely with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation is effective across modalities (vision, language, multimodal) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, retrieval, ranking), but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, availability and nature of distillation data, and task-specific design choices. Practical deployments therefore emphasize task-aware selection of distilled signals, pretraining of compact models, and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Bates
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically oriented set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory use, latency, and communication while often retaining much of task performance. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple logit/soft-target matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, data‑ and privacy‑aware protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success is highly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and choice of distillation data (or synthetic alternatives), and explicit handling of transferred biases, low‑frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Practical deployments treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines, applying task‑aware objective design, layer mapping, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or adapts large or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, generative models, and domain- or privacy-constrained settings, a diverse toolbox has been developed—soft-label supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, self- and online-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and architecture-aware adaptations (e.g., pruning, layer skipping, NAS). Empirical results show that appropriately designed KD pipelines can produce compact models that approach teacher performance and enable deployment in resource-constrained environments, while practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and optimization design. Remaining challenges include principled theory linking teacher signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous architectures or non-iid data, privacy-and-fairness-aware protocols, and extending KD to complex generative and structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Whitney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically grounded family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses a spectrum of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals, and synthetic-data protocols) and workflows (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free, and federated). Empirical results across vision, language, speech, detection, and generative tasks show KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and fidelity, objective selection, and explicit handling of teacher artifacts (biases, low-frequency behavior) and distribution shift. Because of these dependencies, KD is best applied as a configurable, integrated element of compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness and fairness—rather than as a one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Schwartz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a diverse set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and specialized domains, KD methods routinely enable substantial reductions in inference cost and parameter footprint while often retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful selection of distillation targets, alignment of teacher and student architectures, and appropriate data strategies; KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression primitives and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), by how teachers and students are arranged (offline, online, ensemble, self-distillation), and by how distillation is integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free regimes). KD often preserves much of a teacher’s performance and can improve robustness or generalization in some settings, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful handling of bias, distribution shift, and privacy considerations.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger, often ensemble, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational and contrastive objectives—and across protocols including offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, curriculum-guided, and data‑free regimes. Empirical work shows KD routinely improves student efficiency–accuracy trade‑offs when combined with deployment‑aware choices and complementary compression methods. However, reliable deployment requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data regime, optimization and capacity gaps, and risks such as bias transfer and degraded modeling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Stokes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied, pragmatic toolkit for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks the field has developed a diverse taxonomy of transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline, online/self, multi-teacher, data‑free), and integrations with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost, but practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity, handling limited or mismatched data, and mitigating risks such as transferred biases, privacy leakage, and degraded rare-output behavior.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, compute, privacy). Across vision, language, speech, retrieval, and multimodal tasks, KD can preserve much of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student design are chosen for the target task and constraints. Practical KD pipelines combine multiple transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps), complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and data-side interventions (augmentation, synthetic or data-free approaches). However, KD is context dependent: its effectiveness hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and match of transfer data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, rare-case degradation, or privacy risks. Open problems remain around principled theory of transfer, reliable distillation under limited or private data, and automated task-adaptive co-design of teachers, students, and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Serrano
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal settings, KD methods — from soft‑target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi‑teacher and online schemes, and data‑free or privacy‑aware protocols — consistently improve accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when combined with task‑aware design and complementary compression techniques. Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful attention to teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, what signals are transferred and how layers are mapped, data availability or synthesis strategies, and interventions to mitigate bias, rare‑token degradation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and deployment barriers. Methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures; protocols include offline teacher–student training, online or mutual distillation, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free or privacy‑aware workflows. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that also draws on pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies. While KD frequently retains much of a teacher's performance and can improve student generalization, its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and careful mitigation of transferred errors, biases, and distributional mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Myers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD offers a wide set of distillation signals and protocols that generalize across modalities and deployment scenarios, but its success is conditional on teacher and student design, data regime, and integration with complementary compression methods. For reliable, robust deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD operates via many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, adversarial or data‑free generation, and online or multi‑teacher training—and is typically combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet practical latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware design, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful engineering to avoid failure modes such as teacher error transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and recommender systems, KD methods have been developed to match outputs (soft targets), internal representations (features and attention), relational or contrastive signals, and task-specific rank or ordering information. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability (including data-free strategies), and integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Trade-offs include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and optimization challenges; many works propose curricula, student-friendly teacher training, or multi-teacher and online protocols to mitigate these issues. The field has matured into a central engineering primitive for deployment, while continuing to pursue principled transfer objectives, privacy-aware distillation, and robust domain- and architecture-aware pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Fuller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — Toward Integrated, Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students to achieve deployable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its transfer objectives, teacher–student compatibility, and data strategy are chosen to match task constraints, but it also has well-documented failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and poor transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors). For reliable production use, KD should be treated as the configurable core of a broader compression pipeline that integrates representation-aware transfers, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, together with monitoring and mitigation for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Cooke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, speech, detection, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—enable substantial efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, data strategy, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression (e.g., pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Practical deployments use task-aware adaptations, confidence- or curriculum-based weighting, and privacy- or federated-aware designs; remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, distribution shift, rare-output transfer, and principled theory for optimal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted and versatile family of methods for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal tasks. The literature converges on a toolbox of distillation objectives (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or generative approaches), multiple data regimes (full-data, few-shot/limited-data, and data-free/zero-shot), and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers most teacher performance and can act as both information transfer and regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, choice of transfer signals, and data availability. Remaining practical challenges include teacher–student mismatch, transfer of teacher errors or biases, preserving low-frequency and structured outputs, privacy- and federated-learning constraints, and automating task-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Distillation can transfer many types of knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive signals) and can be adapted to scenarios that lack original training data, require privacy guarantees, or demand task- and hardware-aware compression. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, architecture search, pretraining, or ensemble teaching), KD enables large reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving performance. Nevertheless, distillation can propagate biases and teacher artifacts and needs targeted remedies (feature-focused objectives, multi-teacher strategies, teacher annealing, or exposure to raw data) to avoid failure modes on rare phenomena. The literature demonstrates both the breadth of KD methods and concrete best practices to maximize effectiveness across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practically driven family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Over the past decade the literature has developed and evaluated many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), training protocols (offline, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot, and self-distillation), and integrations with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical evidence shows KD often enables substantial gains in inference cost, latency, and memory while recovering much of teacher performance, but reliable application depends on careful, task-aware choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategy (including synthetic or data-free regimes), and explicit mitigations for failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, and propagation of teacher artifacts. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a plug-and-play cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a central, flexible tool for compressing deep and NLP models, but not as a turnkey solution. When designed as a configurable, task‑aware part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and careful data and evaluation strategies—KD routinely delivers strong efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs. Reliable deployment requires explicit mitigation of failure modes (teacher–student capacity mismatch, transferred biases, data scarcity, and distribution shift) and empirical evaluation of robustness, fairness, and rare‑case performance.

papers_seen.author: Beard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance and functionality of larger teacher models. KD is highly versatile—operating at the level of logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational objectives—and is effective across modalities (vision, language, speech, recommender systems, and generative models). However, its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and distribution, and the design of distillation objectives; consequently KD should be treated as a configurable component that is combined with complementary compression techniques and deployment-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, more efficient students while preserving predictive behavior and, in many cases, improving deployment properties such as latency, memory use, privacy, and robustness. The field has expanded from matching teacher logits to a broad set of signals and workflows — internal feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free generation, curriculum and selective-sample protocols, meta- and online-teaching schemes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows that what to transfer (outputs vs. intermediate representations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors), and which data to use (authentic, distilled, augmented, or synthetic) materially affect student outcomes. Practical deployments require task-aware design: align signals to student capacity, mitigate teacher error propagation, handle low-resource or privacy-constrained settings, and combine KD with complementary compression techniques. Remaining challenges include principled theory for which teacher signals are most informative across tasks, reliable transfer under data heterogeneity and domain shift, and preserving rare or structured outputs in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Duran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression — Powerful but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, practically proven approach for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory use, and energy while preserving much of task performance. KD excels when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful teacher–student alignment, and appropriate data strategies; however, it is not a universal remedy. Reliable deployment requires treating KD as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines with explicit provisions for teacher quality, data scarcity, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns.
