papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational constraints), can be adapted to data‑limited and data‑free regimes, and combines productively with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). However, reliable deployment requires task‑aware design: selecting appropriate distillation objectives, aligning teacher and student capacities and architectures, addressing data regimes and privacy constraints, and mitigating failure modes such as bias transfer and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena. Treated as a configurable core of compression pipelines and paired with targeted algorithmic and engineering practices, KD enables practical, deployable model compression across modalities and settings.

papers_seen.author: Schmidt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile technique for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with task‑aware design, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression methods; however, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors, biases, and low‑frequency failures. Treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Mejia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Tool Best Used in a Compression Portfolio
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical syntheses show KD can preserve much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost, but its effectiveness is strongly context-dependent: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, the choice of transfer targets, and careful alignment between teacher and student. Best practice treats KD as a core component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design—and demands task-aware protocols and safeguards for robustness, rare-token behavior, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Reese
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context-Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. KD reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data constraints. However, KD is not automatic: its benefits depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and complementary compression methods; it also requires safeguards to avoid propagating teacher errors or biases. When treated as a configurable component of compression pipelines and paired with targeted techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and selection of transfer signals), KD is the most practical first-line strategy for many deployment scenarios in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical toolkit for converting large teacher models or ensembles into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, privacy, and deployment constraints. A rich family of distillation targets and training protocols has emerged—soft logits, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, data‑free and adversarial synthesis, and federated or online variants. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with task‑aware choices about signals to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, and appropriate data strategies, but it has well-documented limits (capacity mismatch, teacher error/bias propagation, degraded long‑tail/rare-token behavior, distribution shift, and data- or privacy-limited regimes). Robust, deployable compression therefore treats KD as a configurable core component embedded in an integrated pipeline with complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and explicit safeguards and evaluation for fairness, robustness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models. KD routinely yields large efficiency gains (reduced memory, compute, and latency) while preserving much of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher quality, student capacity, data availability (including privacy or data‑free regimes), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and degraded handling of rare phenomena. Treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with targeted algorithmic and engineering practices, KD enables practical, deployable compression across modalities and settings.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple teacher-to-student logit matching into a broad toolkit for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models across vision, language, multimodal, and structured domains. Modern KD transfers soft targets, intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, or synthesized data; it operates in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while reducing compute, memory, and latency, but success depends on teacher quality, capacity matching, data/augmentation strategy, and careful design of objectives and layer mappings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, applications, and practical recommendations documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal domains, a diverse set of distillation targets (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational structure) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, data‑free or self‑distillation) have been developed. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover much of a teacher’s performance while enabling lower latency, reduced memory use, and new deployment modes; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful design of the transfer objective. Practical pipelines commonly pair KD with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task‑aware procedures (layer mapping, curriculum, teacher adaptation) to meet deployment constraints. Important open problems include robust transfer under distribution shift and data scarcity, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, principled automated design for heterogeneous student architectures, and privacy‑aware or data‑free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default First‑Line, Configurable Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact student models from larger teachers. KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, and it supports many transfer targets and training paradigms. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data regime, and the choice of distilled signals. The recommended position is to adopt KD as the default first-line compression strategy but to embed it in an integrated, task-aware pipeline that combines complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), data strategies (including data-free or synthetic data when needed), projector and layer-mapping designs, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teacher models. KD methods span output-level supervision, intermediate representation matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-aware or data-free protocols. While KD routinely yields favorable trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness, its success is strongly context dependent: choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability and synthesis, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy determine practical outcomes. As a result, KD should be treated as a configurable, first‑line element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Short
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A broad set of objectives and protocols—logit-level supervision, feature/attention alignment, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial or synthesized-data methods, and online or multi-teacher schemes—has been developed and is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Practical effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and targeted engineering (layer mapping, projectors, curriculum), and remaining challenges include teacher-bias propagation, data-domain mismatch, optimization instability, and preserving low-frequency behaviors in structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Briggs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a mature, flexible family of techniques that enables deployment of compact models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teachers. When applied as a configurable element within an integrated compression pipeline and coupled with careful teacher–student co‑design, data strategies, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), distillation reliably improves efficiency while often preserving most of the teacher’s performance. However, effectiveness is context dependent: practitioner choices about what to transfer, how to generate or select data, and how to mitigate transferred errors, bias, or distribution shift determine real-world outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Ashley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Patterns, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD variants include matching teacher logits, imitating intermediate representations, aligning attention or relational structures, ensembling multiple teachers, adversarial and data-free distillation, and student- or task-aware curricula. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapted for settings with limited or private data, federated training, and non‑standard outputs (e.g., generative or structured prediction). Empirically, thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and in many cases enable practical deployment trade-offs, but they are not universally effective: success depends on student capacity, data and distribution match, choice of teacher signals, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare‑phenomena degradation. Ongoing research focuses on principled objectives, robust and private distillation, and task‑aware architectures for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Vaughan
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring knowledge from large, high‑capacity teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how transfer is organized (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, or data‑free), and how they are integrated with other compression tools (pruning, quantization, neural architecture search, progressive module replacement). When carefully applied and combined with task‑aware choices about data, layer alignment, and auxiliary compression, KD frequently yields compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency and memory. However, KD is context dependent: success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and mitigation of failure modes such as propagation of teacher errors, degraded rare‑token behavior, distribution shift, and privacy concerns. The field emphasizes engineering pipelines that pair KD with complementary strategies and targeted remedies rather than a single universal recipe.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applied approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data‑free or online protocols. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks. Effective deployment treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and careful data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Banks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teacher models. KD transfers information at multiple levels—soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational maps, and synthesized examples—and is commonly integrated with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, or privacy, but its success is conditional on task‑aware design, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as distributional shift, propagation of teacher errors, long‑tail degradation, and privacy/fairness concerns. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a universal cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Watson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a versatile and widely applied means of producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, multimodal and distributed settings. It offers many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals), multiple protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free), and can be combined with pruning, quantization and architecture search to meet real deployment constraints. However, KD’s empirical success is conditional: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and explicit measures to mitigate bias, low‑frequency behaviors and distributional shift determine whether students approach teacher performance. Treated as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and paired with targeted data, evaluation and robustness safeguards, KD is the most practical route to deployable compressed models; treated as a plug‑and‑play cure, it frequently falls short.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Practical, but Insufficiently Complete Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a practical and flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. It supports multiple transfer targets (logits, features, attention, relational signals), multi-teacher and data-free setups, and integrates naturally with complementary compression methods. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and task-aware objective design. To realize KD’s full potential in real-world deployments, practitioners must treat it as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for transferring predictive behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of the original performance. KD spans logits-based supervision, feature and relational matching, adversarial or synthetic data generation, and architectural or curriculum adaptations. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are aligned, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD can enable deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings and sometimes yield students that match or exceed teacher performance, but it also carries risks—propagating teacher errors and biases, struggling under data scarcity or mismatch, and requiring task-specific engineering. I argue KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines, applied conditionally with targeted remedies and validated against task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Morton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, flexible paradigm for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so they can be deployed under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. When designed with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search), distillation routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance. However, distillation is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the distillation signals chosen; it can propagate teacher artifacts and struggles with optimization gaps, capacity mismatch, and low-frequency behavior. Addressing these limits requires joint teacher–student design, confidence- or curriculum-aware sample selection, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis when data are unavailable, and incorporation into broader compression pipelines tailored to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Martinez

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware design, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful engineering to avoid failure modes such as teacher error transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Bartlett
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, broadly applicable family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models from larger teacher models. Empirical evidence across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains shows that KD—particularly when combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and when guided by task‑aware objectives and data strategies—regularly yields favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs. papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Dependent, Foundational Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses many mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, data‑free and multi‑teacher schemes) and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, curriculum, domain adaptation). Its power for deployment in resource‑ or privacy‑constrained settings is well documented; however, KD is not universally sufficient. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher‑student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, bias transfer, and degradation on rare phenomena. papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision and language modalities. A wide range of distillation signals (soft logits, internal features, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives), workflows (offline, online, multi-teacher, teacher‑free), and data strategies (authentic, augmented, or synthetic) have been developed and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the selection or synthesis of distillation data, and targeted mitigation of transferred biases or distribution-shift failures.

papers_seen.author: Burns
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Context‑Dependent

papers_seen.author: Gallegos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Configurable Core of Hybrid Model‑Compression Pipelines

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Arnold

papers_seen.author: Scott

papers_seen.author: Wise

papers_seen.author: Hernandez

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD routinely achieves strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities and tasks when its objectives, teacher–student design, data strategies, and complementary compression methods are chosen with deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution, and explicit safeguards against bias, robustness, and privacy failures. Best practice treats KD as a configurable building block embedded in an integrated compression pipeline tailored to the task and environment.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to compact student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels of supervision, support varied training protocols, and are commonly integrated with complementary compression primitives to satisfy latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Practical success depends on careful choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness and fairness; remaining challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors, and principled guidance for heterogeneous architectures and federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Quinn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Not Sufficient — A Case for Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated toolkit that transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. KD methods span soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-aware or data-free schemes. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher capability and enables deployment under resource and privacy constraints, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the distillation signals chosen, and the data regime. Consequently, KD is best treated as a central, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and careful data and evaluation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, a broad toolkit of distillation targets and protocols has been developed and combined with complementary compression methods to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Success is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and careful task-aware design determine how much teacher performance is preserved and what tradeoffs arise.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a simple teacher-to-student logit-matching recipe into a diverse toolkit that addresses compression, cross-model transfer, domain adaptation, privacy, and deployment constraints. Across vision, language, multimodal, and structured domains, methods that transfer internal representations, align features across layers, leverage adversarial or boundary-focused samples, or synthesize distilled training data enable smaller models to approximate or even match larger models on task performance while meeting latency, fairness, and interpretability demands. Effective use of KD depends on matching the distillation paradigm to the target problem: use internal/feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP tasks, layer- and task-aware filters when capacity mismatch is large, adversarial or boundary-focused sampling to improve generalization, and data-free or federated-aware strategies when data access is restricted. Combining KD with pruning and hardware-aware compression further increases suitability for edge deployment.

papers_seen.author: Fleming
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical family of methods for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The literature documents diverse distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), multiple training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free methods), and many integrations with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). Empirical evidence shows KD—when matched to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, and data conditions—can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on careful selection of transfer signals and objectives, appropriate teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including augmentation and synthetic/data‑free approaches), and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, capacity gaps, transferred biases, and distribution shift. Ongoing open problems include formalizing when particular KD signals preserve generalization, distilling reliably under scarce or private data, and principled mitigation of harmful transferred behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Roach
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods span output-level supervision (soft logits), intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive losses, adversarial and data-free generation, online and multi-teacher protocols, and self-distillation. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks shows KD frequently yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are carefully matched. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline alongside pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and calls for explicit strategies to mitigate teacher bias, handle data scarcity or privacy constraints, and maintain rare-token or long-tail behaviors. Remaining challenges include principled signal selection for heterogeneous architectures, robust and private distillation under non‑i.i.d. data, and automated, deployment‑aware teacher–student co‑design.

papers_seen.author: Thornton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation Is Essential but Context‑Sensitive for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely adopted toolkit for producing compact models that approach the performance of larger teachers. KD routinely delivers favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across modalities when it is chosen and configured with attention to what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and the available data regime. However, KD is not a universal panacea: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability (or synthesis), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degraded long‑tail/low‑frequency behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Leon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Configurable Core of Integrated Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, versatile set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across modalities. Empirical evidence shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but its reliability is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regime, and the chosen distillation targets and protocol determine outcomes. For robust, deployment-ready compression, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and fairness/privacy safeguards—rather than a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to satisfy deployment constraints such as latency, memory, compute, and privacy. KD includes a wide set of objectives and training protocols (logits/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, online/multi-teacher schemes, and data‑free or synthesized-data approaches). Empirical work shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance when it is matched to student capacity and data regimes and when it is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). At the same time, KD has clear limits—teacher–student mismatch, scarce or mismatched data, propagation of teacher errors and biases, and difficulty preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors—so best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline with explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative tasks. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, features, attention, or generated data), data strategy, and teacher–student alignment, KD routinely yields substantial inference and memory gains while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is bounded by data availability, teacher quality, capacity mismatch, and potential transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors, so it is best used as part of an integrated compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Crawford
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods that transfer knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses diverse transfer targets and training protocols and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design. Empirical evidence across modalities shows substantial efficiency gains, but persistent challenges—data limitations, capacity mismatch, transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors, and degradation on long-tail phenomena—motivate careful pipeline design and continued research on robust, privacy-aware, and hardware-aware distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. When combined with pre-training, careful choice of distillation signals, data- and task-aware strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture replacement), KD produces compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, availability or synthesis of data, alignment of internal representations, and consideration of fairness and robustness. Best practice therefore treats KD as a flexible toolkit—mixing soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-level matching, online/ensemble schemes, and domain-aware adjustments—to meet practical production requirements.

papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers, but it is not a standalone cure-all. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and representations across modalities when chosen and tuned with regard to teacher quality, student capacity, data regimes, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—while adopting safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically proven family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD spans outputs-only approaches (soft targets) to rich objectives that match intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, or contrastive signals. It operates across many data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free, synthetic-data), and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to achieve deployment constraints on latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity. The effectiveness of KD is strongly context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies (including augmentation, curriculum, and synthetic generation). Common failure modes include propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors, and optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, motivating targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Herring
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, many-to-many layer mappings, projector-based feature transforms, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis — enables large reductions in parameters and inference cost while often preserving much of teacher performance. Successful application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle data availability and privacy, and how to combine KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning and quantization. Remaining research challenges include principled theory for objective selection, reliable transfer under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Jacobson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Empirical Findings, Methods, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of methods for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings, KD variants (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate feature and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free protocols) routinely yield favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with task-aware design. Practical deployment benefits from integrating KD with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic data, multi-teacher ensembles). However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and heterogeneity, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, low-frequency behavior loss, and distribution-shift fragility. Future progress requires principled choices of distilled signals, automated teacher–student alignment, reliable distillation under scarce or private data, and tighter theory connecting distillation objectives to generalization and robustness.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD spans simple soft-target (logit) matching to richer objectives that align intermediate representations, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and decision boundaries; it also includes online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data‑free variants. Across vision, language, graphs, speech, detection, and generative modeling, KD routinely yields favorable trade-offs between efficiency and performance when it is matched to student capacity, teacher quality, and the available data. Practical success typically requires integrating KD into a broader compression pipeline (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis/augmentation) and explicitly addressing teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, distribution shift, and the risk of transferring undesirable behaviors. Key open directions include principled signal selection for heterogeneous architectures, robust data‑free and privacy‑preserving distillation, and automated, deployment‑aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practically driven family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Over the past decade the literature has developed and evaluated many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), training protocols (offline, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot, and self-distillation), and integrations with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical evidence shows KD often enables substantial gains in inference cost, latency, and memory while recovering much of teacher performance, but reliable application depends on careful, task-aware choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategy (including synthetic or data-free regimes), and explicit mitigations for failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, and propagation of teacher artifacts. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a plug-and-play cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware toolkit and combined with complementary compression methods, distillation enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy; it must be applied conditionally with safeguards against error and bias propagation.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practically oriented set of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants transfer information at the level of logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, and are commonly combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Empirical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance under resource or privacy constraints, but success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and match of transfer data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as teacher error/bias propagation, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and sensitivity to distribution shift. Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component within an integrated compression pipeline yields the most robust, deployable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Component: Toward Task‑Aware, Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable mechanism for transferring capabilities from large teacher models into smaller student models, enabling significant reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while preserving much of task performance. However, KD alone cannot address all deployment concerns: it can propagate teacher errors and biases, struggle under data scarcity or distribution shift, and fail to deliver hardware‑optimal compression. The most reliable production strategies treat KD as a central, configurable element within a broader, task‑aware compression pipeline that combines careful teacher–student design, data strategies (including data‑free or synthetic data), and complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture adaptations to meet robustness, fairness, privacy, and hardware constraints.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for transferring functionality from large teacher models to smaller students so that compressed models retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and communication. KD covers a spectrum of techniques—from soft-target matching to internal representation transfer, multi-teacher/online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and architecture-aware solutions such as task-adaptive compression—and integrates naturally with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). When implemented with care about teacher selection, data selection or synthesis, and representation alignment, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing models across modalities; when misapplied it can propagate teacher errors, amplify biases, or fail due to optimization and data-mismatch issues. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-order engineering primitive for model compression in deep learning and NLP, and outlines recommended practices and known limitations to guide responsible adoption.

papers_seen.author: Reyes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Core of Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows that KD often preserves much of teacher performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count; however, its success is context dependent and it must be integrated with complementary compression, data, and safety strategies for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable set of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers. When combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and tailored to task and data constraints, KD unlocks deployment on latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained platforms while supporting modalities from language to vision and multimodal systems. However, KD is not automatic: careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors (bias, rare-token degradation) are required for responsible, robust outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Reyes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings, practitioners use KD to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Modern distillation extends beyond matching output probabilities to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware choices, pruning, quantization, curriculum or data strategies, and safeguards for fairness and robustness. Remaining challenges include teacher–student capacity mismatch, distributional and low-frequency phenomena, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and principled automation of distillation design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer behavior and/or internal structure from larger, often ensemble or multi-modal teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to intermediate-feature, attention, and relational matching—and are widely used to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory or latency constraints, and support domain or modality adaptation. The effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and careful design of what and how knowledge is transferred; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and targeted training protocols improves reliability in practice.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.
