papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applied method for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller students. KD variants (logits, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free and federated protocols) have enabled practical deployment across vision, language, retrieval, generative modeling, and healthcare. However, KD faces concrete limitations—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity or privacy constraints, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and potential fairness or robustness regressions—that reduce its effectiveness when used alone. The strongest practical outcomes come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful selection or synthesis of distilled supervision, and task- and data-aware training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes what the provided literature collectively reports about knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques: commonly used distillation objectives and training protocols, empirical patterns of when and how KD helps across modalities, practical constraints and failure modes (data availability, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency/structured outputs, privacy and bias transfer), and targeted solutions (data-free/zero-shot distillation, teacher engineering, multi-teacher and curriculum schemes, and combinations with pruning/quantization and architecture search). The goal is to give a concise map of methods, observed trade-offs, and open problems for researchers and practitioners working on compressing or adapting large models for resource- or deployment-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Haynes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, Practical Strategies, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while preserving much of task performance. The literature shows a broad toolkit—soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and layer-mapping objectives, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and multi-teacher or self-distillation protocols—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical evidence indicates KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve low-precision and deployment behavior, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful alignment of objectives and training procedures. Open problems remain around robustness, distribution shift, low-frequency behavior, fairness, and principled design of teacher–student pairings and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques encompass output-level supervision (soft logits), representation- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, progressive module replacement, and online or multi-teacher protocols. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost, but success is context-sensitive: it depends on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and distribution of data (including data-free or synthesized alternatives), and careful loss and layer-mapping choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable toolbox to be combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-, fairness-, or privacy-aware interventions. Remaining scientific and engineering challenges include principled selection of distillation targets, reliable distillation under limited or mismatched data, mitigation of transferred biases and rare-token degradation, theoretical understanding of when and why different KD objectives help, and automated, hardware-aware co-design for heterogeneous deployment.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to satisfy deployment constraints such as latency, memory, compute, and privacy. KD includes a wide set of objectives and training protocols (logits/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, online/multi-teacher schemes, and data‑free or synthesized-data approaches). Empirical work shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance when it is matched to student capacity and data regimes and when it is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). At the same time, KD has clear limits—teacher–student mismatch, scarce or mismatched data, propagation of teacher errors and biases, and difficulty preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors—so best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline with explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Pitts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. KD techniques span soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level objectives, relational/contrastive signals, and protocols such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free variants. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks KD routinely reduces latency, memory, and compute while recovering much of teacher performance, but its success is context-dependent: outcomes hinge on signal choice, teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression primitives. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of broader compression pipelines, guided by task-aware design, teacher–student co‑engineering, and targeted mitigations for bias, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Fleming
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical family of methods for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The literature documents diverse distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), multiple training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free methods), and many integrations with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). Empirical evidence shows KD—when matched to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, and data conditions—can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on careful selection of transfer signals and objectives, appropriate teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including augmentation and synthetic/data‑free approaches), and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, capacity gaps, transferred biases, and distribution shift. Ongoing open problems include formalizing when particular KD signals preserve generalization, distilling reliably under scarce or private data, and principled mitigation of harmful transferred behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, versatile toolkit for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from high-capacity teachers to smaller students. Empirical evidence across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows KD frequently recovers much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategy, and the complementary compression techniques used. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than as a standalone, universal recipe.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Santana
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, more efficient student models. KD reduces inference cost, memory footprint, and communication overhead while often preserving much of the teacher’s performance across vision, language, speech, generation, and multimodal tasks. Its practical value arises when KD is designed around task objectives, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints, and when it is combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted framework for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative modeling, and multimodal tasks, KD methods trade off accuracy, latency, and resource use by transferring different forms of information (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, or synthesized training examples). Empirical work shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve generalization and deployment feasibility, but KD has practical limits tied to teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, bias transfer, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment mixes careful choice of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, multi-teacher or confidence-weighting schemes, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate across multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure) and training paradigms (offline, online/multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free/adversarial synthesis). Empirical work shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and compute constraints, but its success is context‑dependent and typically benefits from integration with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic data, data‑free approaches), and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Frazier
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically proven family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into compact students. KD reduces inference cost and memory and supports a wide range of transfer targets and training regimes. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and selection, and design choices; for robust, fair, and production-ready compression it should be integrated with complementary techniques and targeted safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Haynes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, Practical Strategies, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while preserving much of task performance. The literature shows a broad toolkit—soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and layer-mapping objectives, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and multi-teacher or self-distillation protocols—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical evidence indicates KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve low-precision and deployment behavior, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful alignment of objectives and training procedures. Open problems remain around robustness, distribution shift, low-frequency behavior, fairness, and principled design of teacher–student pairings and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted strategy for producing smaller, faster, or more interpretable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact student models. A wide range of techniques has been developed that go beyond matching final outputs to include intermediate representation matching, attention/feature imitation, contrastive and relational objectives, and architecture-aware optimization; KD is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning demonstrates that careful selection of teacher signals, student capacity, data regimes, and auxiliary compression methods strongly affects final trade-offs between efficiency and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of KD objectives and workflows—soft-target matching, intermediate-representation mimicking, relational or attention-map transfer, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and applied across vision, language, graph, and recommendation settings. Empirical and theoretical work demonstrates substantial practical gains in latency, memory, and deployability when KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping), but success depends on careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objective design; remaining challenges include optimization difficulties, distribution shift, rare-token performance, and bias or privacy leakage.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). The field has developed a broad toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, and teacher-student co-training — that has been applied across vision, language, multimodal, detection, segmentation, and federated settings. Empirical work shows distilled models can often recover much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost; success depends on student capacity, alignment of inputs and layers, availability and nature of distillation data, and choices about what form of knowledge to transfer. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and task-aware adaptations; outstanding challenges include principled theory, reliable distillation under data or device heterogeneity and privacy constraints, transferring rare or structured outputs, and automating teacher/student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Ponce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models across vision, language, speech, and other modalities. KD methods operate over multiple signals and protocols and are most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that also addresses data, architecture, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or structural information. A broad toolkit of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online/self-, multi-teacher, data‑free) and engineering practices (layer mapping, projectors, curriculum, data synthesis) has been developed and routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirically, distillation frequently recovers most of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and augmentation strategies, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to integrate distillation within end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks KD routinely yields substantial gains in inference efficiency while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance, but its success is conditional on teacher–student design, data regime, and complementary compression choices. Practical use treats KD as a configurable component of broader compression pipelines that also draw on pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or specialized models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble and multi-teacher schemes, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and layer-mapping strategies — and these methods are combined routinely with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation is effective across modalities (vision, language, multimodal) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, retrieval, ranking), but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, availability and nature of distillation data, and task-specific design choices. Practical deployments therefore emphasize task-aware selection of distilled signals, pretraining of compact models, and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, researchers have applied KD for inference speedup, deployment on resource-constrained devices, privacy-preserving model release, and enhanced robustness or interpretability. Methods vary from standard teacher–student soft-label supervision to data-free distillation, adversarially chosen boundary samples, many-to-many layer mappings, generative replay, and architecture-aware compression. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when combined with task-aware design, careful sample selection, and appropriate optimization; challenges remain around distributional mismatch, low-frequency token handling, heterogeneous architectures, and privacy/validation in data-free scenarios. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compressed models, joint optimization of pruning and KD, federated/distilled learning across heterogeneous devices, and cross-modal distillation for generative capabilities.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. KD routinely delivers large gains in latency and memory while retaining much of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and student architectures are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a plug‑and‑play cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, the nature and availability of data, and careful mitigation of transferred errors, robustness gaps, and fairness/privacy risks. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data strategies—to achieve reliable, responsible deployment.

papers_seen.author: Dominguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of methods for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and other modalities KD variants (logits/soft-targets, intermediate features, attention or relational transfers, and data‑synthesis/data‑free approaches) enable substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while often preserving most of a teacher’s performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and careful data or privacy strategies—and when practitioners attend to teacher–student compatibility, data regime, and task constraints. Known limitations include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, sensitivity to distribution shift and rare/low-frequency phenomena, and optimization or alignment challenges that require method selection and safeguards tailored to deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are essential for deploying high-performing deep models under resource constraints. Empirical evidence across vision, speech, and NLP shows that combining sensible pre-training, careful choice of distillation signals (outputs and internal representations), appropriate training data or augmentation, and dynamic teacher-student strategies yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy. Complementary techniques — online or mutual distillation, data-free and federated distillation, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-distillation — further extend applicability to privacy-constrained, multi-domain, and large-scale training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Conditional — Toward Task‑Aware, Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers information at many levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and supports a wide range of protocols (offline teacher→student, online co‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free or privacy‑aware schemes). Empirical evidence shows KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends on task awareness, teacher–student alignment, student capacity, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Best practice therefore treats KD as the configurable core of a broader compression pipeline that combines appropriate distillation objectives with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies) tailored to the target task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable, task‑aware component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with data strategies, architecture design, and complementary techniques such as pruning and quantization—rather than as a one‑size‑fits‑all recipe. Its strengths include strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks and support for privacy- or data‑limited settings; its limits include teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatches, optimization and distribution‑shift failures, and degradation on rare or fine‑grained outputs. Practical deployment requires explicit attention to what signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how distillation is integrated with other compression and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Carter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses approaches that match teacher outputs (soft logits), intermediate features or attention, relational and contrastive signals, and methods that operate with or without access to original training data. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and matched to task- and data-specific constraints, KD routinely yields substantial reductions in parameters and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. However, effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, choice of distilled signals, data availability and preparation, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Important open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, reliable distillation under limited or private data, mitigation of bias transfer, and theory connecting distilled signals to student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining much of the teacher’s performance. The literature shows a diverse toolkit of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure, channel statistics, and contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free variants), and task-aware adaptations (layer mapping, projector modules, synthetic-data generation, and curriculum/annealing). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, multimodal tasks, and continual or federated settings demonstrates substantial efficiency gains but also highlights persistent challenges: teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatch, limited or unavailable training data, propagation of teacher biases or errors, distribution shift, and difficulties transferring rare or low-frequency behaviors. Practical success typically requires matching the distillation signal to task and student capacity and integrating KD with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective and versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Its practical strengths include enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints and supporting a wide range of transfer targets and training protocols. However, distillation outcomes depend strongly on task context, teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and augmentation, and explicit handling of transferred errors and biases. For reliable, production‑ready compression, knowledge distillation should be treated as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines appropriate distillation signals with complementary techniques and safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Morse
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical framework for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks. A rich toolkit of distillation targets and protocols has been developed—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, multi- and self-distillation, and online or federated variants. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing parameters, latency, and memory, but outcomes are strongly context-dependent: success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and synthesis strategies, and careful mitigation of teacher errors, distribution shift, and privacy or fairness risks. Combining KD with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation/search) and tailoring distillation signals to the task produces the most robust practical results. Remaining gaps include principled theory linking transfer signals to generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneity and domain shift, and preserving structured or rare outputs in complex sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a rich, task-sensitive toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to compact students. Practitioners move beyond simple logit matching to transfer internal representations, attention patterns, relational structure, and decision-boundary information, and they combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Empirical results across vision, language, generative models, and structured prediction show distilled students often recover much of teacher performance and can enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but distillation also has failure modes—teacher bias transfer, sensitivity to data availability, capacity mismatch, and degraded modeling of low-frequency phenomena—that require targeted mitigations and continued theoretical and empirical work.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures, and they operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align layers, and how to handle limited or private data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, robustness and fairness transfer, data-free/privacy-preserving distillation, and principled selection of distilled signals.

papers_seen.author: Vaughan
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring knowledge from large, high‑capacity teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how transfer is organized (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, or data‑free), and how they are integrated with other compression tools (pruning, quantization, neural architecture search, progressive module replacement). When carefully applied and combined with task‑aware choices about data, layer alignment, and auxiliary compression, KD frequently yields compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency and memory. However, KD is context dependent: success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and mitigation of failure modes such as propagation of teacher errors, degraded rare‑token behavior, distribution shift, and privacy concerns. The field emphasizes engineering pipelines that pair KD with complementary strategies and targeted remedies rather than a single universal recipe.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques encompass output-level supervision (soft logits), representation- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, progressive module replacement, and online or multi-teacher protocols. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost, but success is context-sensitive: it depends on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and distribution of data (including data-free or synthesized alternatives), and careful loss and layer-mapping choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable toolbox to be combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-, fairness-, or privacy-aware interventions. Remaining scientific and engineering challenges include principled selection of distillation targets, reliable distillation under limited or mismatched data, mitigation of transferred biases and rare-token degradation, theoretical understanding of when and why different KD objectives help, and automated, hardware-aware co-design for heterogeneous deployment.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Contextual Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, broadly applicable set of methods for producing smaller, faster, and deployment-ready models by transferring information from large teacher models into compact students. KD techniques range from soft-label (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and relational objectives, and they have been adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, to multi-teacher or online schemes, and to combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve interpretability or privacy-aware deployment, its success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and distributional constraints. Consequently, KD is best treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a plug-and-play cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Sensitive Core of Integrated Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Treated as a configurable core of compression workflows, KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory footprint while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy are chosen to match task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not a standalone cure: reliable production deployments combine KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), targeted data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or privacy-preserving data), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagated teacher biases, and low-frequency degradation.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Benefits, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient students to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, KD has evolved from simple logits-matching into a configurable toolkit that includes feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance when applied with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and appropriate data strategies; however, important failure modes remain (teacher quality, student capacity, limited data, distribution shift, and propagation of biases), motivating integrated pipelines and targeted mitigation strategies for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Dougherty
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD works at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, relational/contrastive signals, and data‑synthesis protocols) and is most reliable when adapted to task constraints, teacher and student capacity, and available data. I argue that KD should be treated as the central, configurable core of any compression pipeline but not as a standalone cure: to be robust and production‑ready it must be combined with complementary compression primitives, careful layer and signal design, and specific remedies for documented failure modes such as teacher–student mismatch, transferred biases, and degradation on low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD operates via many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, adversarial or data‑free generation, and online or multi‑teacher training—and is typically combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet practical latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware design, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful engineering to avoid failure modes such as teacher error transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Gill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and optimization problems, a consistent empirical story has emerged: carefully designed distillation objectives and workflows can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practical success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, the availability and composition of transfer data, and the use of complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity or privacy, distribution shift, and preserving rare or long-tail phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Spencer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely successful family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost, but its reliability depends on task- and data-aware design choices, teacher–student alignment, and integration with complementary compression primitives. Responsible deployment requires explicit attention to data availability, distributional shift, rare-case behaviors, and fairness or privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Not Panacea Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted technique for compressing large models into smaller ones and transferring capabilities across tasks and modalities. When thoughtfully designed—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), preparing or augmenting data, and matching teacher-student capacity—KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency with modest performance loss and can enable deployment under tight latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and architecture alignment; complementary tools (pretraining, projector modules, online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols) and careful engineering are often required to realize consistent, robust results. Open directions include principled data-free distillation, better theoretical characterizations of what is transferred, and joint co-design of architectures and distillation objectives for specific deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Power, Limits, and Responsible Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models in constrained or sensitive settings. KD transfers information from one or more teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained students via soft targets, intermediate-representation matching, contrastive/objective-level alignment, adversarial schemes, or synthetic-data generation. When designed carefully—choosing suitable teacher signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, integrating augmentation and complementary compression methods, and accounting for domain shift and fairness—KD routinely recovers most of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment modes (edge, federated, privacy-sensitive). However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher–student mismatch, optimization choices, and the potential transfer of undesirable properties (bias, rare-token degradation). Responsible use requires principled teacher selection, careful objective design, augmentation and sample-selection strategies, and techniques for data-free or privacy-preserving scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring capabilities of large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, attention- and projector-based transfers, data-free and zero-shot schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols, and integrations with quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical work across language, vision, 3D perception, retrieval, and federated settings shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is combined with suitable data strategies, teacher design, and complementary compression methods. Important open challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, robust transfer across heterogeneous architectures, and principled selection of what and how to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When properly designed—choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which complementary compression methods to use—KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports a range of practical use cases. However, KD is not turnkey: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability of suitable data (or reliable data synthesis), and careful mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone solution, and I summarize practical recommendations and open challenges that follow from this position.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, multimodal, and generative domains show KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Practical deployment favors combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), choosing appropriate transfer targets (logits, features, attention, decision-boundary signals), and adopting data- and task-aware strategies. KD also has well-documented limitations — optimization obstacles that prevent perfect teacher matching, sensitivity to teacher quality and data regimes, and risks of propagating teacher biases or poor modeling of rare phenomena — which motivate targeted mitigations such as adversarial/sample-selection methods, multi-teacher and teacher-aware schemes, data-free or privacy-preserving formulations, and representation-level objectives. Overall, KD is best viewed as a flexible, task-aware toolkit whose effectiveness depends on matching methods and safeguards to the compression and deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Kelly
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teachers into smaller students. When treated as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines and paired with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthesis, privacy-preserving protocols), KD routinely yields large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. Its success is, however, conditional: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigation of propagated biases, rare-case failures, and distribution shift determine outcomes. Best practice treats KD not as a turnkey cure but as a task‑aware, engineered component of end-to-end compression and evaluation workflows.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact student models. A wide range of distillation objectives (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive losses), training protocols (offline, online/self-, multi-teacher), and data strategies (full-data, limited-data, data-free, and privacy-aware synthesis) have been proposed and combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical studies show KD often recovers much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and suitable data strategies are available, but KD is context-dependent and must be integrated with task-aware design choices to manage limits related to teacher–student mismatch, optimization, data scarcity, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically proven approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. KD methods include logits matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and variants that operate online, with multiple teachers, or without access to original training data. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component within a broader compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies; its benefits and limits depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of bias and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression — Powerful but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods (soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational objectives, and data- or generator-based synthesis) repeatedly enable large reductions in model size and inference cost when combined with task-aware design and complementary compression primitives. However, KD's success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Treating KD as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines, rather than a one-shot cure, leads to more reliable and deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Acosta
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical family of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks. KD methods span matching soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, and extend to online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free and privacy‑aware protocols. Empirical and methodological work shows KD often recovers a substantial fraction of teacher performance when combined with task‑aware choices and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), but its success is context‑sensitive: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of robustness, fairness, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.
