papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature documents a wide family of methods, consistent practical benefits when KD is used thoughtfully, and a set of recurring failure modes that make KD most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques and task‑aware protocol design. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, deployment considerations, and open challenges distilled from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Perkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a flexible, task-aware family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses a range of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free and few-shot), and data strategies (authentic, augmented, synthetic, or generated replay). Empirical work across vision, speech, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows that KD produces meaningful efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and signal selection are aligned; however, KD is not automatic and faces limits from capacity mismatch, teacher artifacts, low-frequency or structured outputs, data heterogeneity, and fairness/privacy concerns. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox that is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single recipe but as a versatile, task-aware toolkit that enables compact, efficient, and deployable models across modalities. KD methods—ranging from logit-based soft targets to feature-, layer-, and relation-level matching, and including self-, multi-teacher, data-free, and online variants—consistently trade small accuracy loss for large gains in latency, memory, and privacy. Reliable application requires careful attention to teacher quality and compatibility, what to transfer, the data regime, and interactions with regularizers and complementary compression methods. When designed around deployment constraints and task objectives, KD delivers practical, often substantial improvements for on-device inference, domain adaptation, federated settings, and robustness-sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Power, Limits, and Responsible Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models in constrained or sensitive settings. KD transfers information from one or more teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained students via soft targets, intermediate-representation matching, contrastive/objective-level alignment, adversarial schemes, or synthetic-data generation. When designed carefully—choosing suitable teacher signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, integrating augmentation and complementary compression methods, and accounting for domain shift and fairness—KD routinely recovers most of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment modes (edge, federated, privacy-sensitive). However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on data availability, teacher–student mismatch, optimization choices, and the potential transfer of undesirable properties (bias, rare-token degradation). Responsible use requires principled teacher selection, careful objective design, augmentation and sample-selection strategies, and techniques for data-free or privacy-preserving scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Wise
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, empirically supported approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. Rather than a one-shot cure, KD is most effective when treated as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that explicitly addresses teacher–student alignment, data strategies, complementary compression techniques, and known failure modes. This position emphasizes KD's practical value, its conditional limits, and a set of operational practices that convert KD's flexibility into reliable, production-ready compression.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated, practical family of methods for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD methods include soft-logit/temperature matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free schemes, and online/self‑distillation variants. In practice KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when training choices account for teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and deployment constraints. KD often preserves most teacher performance and can improve student generalization, but it can also transfer teacher biases or degrade rare-token behavior; therefore it should be treated as a configurable, task-aware component of end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks KD routinely yields substantial gains in inference efficiency while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance, but its success is conditional on teacher–student design, data regime, and complementary compression choices. Practical use treats KD as a configurable component of broader compression pipelines that also draw on pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best-Practice‑Driven for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. KD provides a flexible family of mechanisms (soft-targets, feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free or federated protocols) that, when combined with complementary compression primitives and task-aware design, yield strong empirical trade-offs between efficiency and performance. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. A broad toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (real, synthetic, or data‑free) has been developed. KD is routinely combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and can be adapted to privacy‑sensitive or data-limited regimes. Empirically, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities, but success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and targeted mitigation for transferred errors, distribution shift, and social harms. Treating KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all recipe—yields the most reliable, deployable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Configurable Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals), diverse scheduling regimes (offline, online, progressive), and synergistic combination with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest loss in task performance, its success is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability (or synthetic/data-free strategies), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, robustness, and privacy concerns determine outcomes. Consequently, KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable tool in compression pipelines—selected and tuned according to task, data, and deployment constraints—rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Mata
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Practical, but Context‑Dependent for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When designed to match the task, data regime, and student capacity, KD routinely preserves much of teacher performance and enables deployment under compute, latency, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on careful choice of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and loss of rare behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve calibration, robustness, or task adaptation. The field has evolved from logits-based soft-target training to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free approaches, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, handling limited or mismatched data, and explicitly addressing risks such as transferred biases or privacy leakage. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a single turnkey algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context‑Sensitive Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. It routinely yields large efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance, but its effectiveness is strongly context-dependent: success requires task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle data and deployment constraints, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression primitives. Treating distillation as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline produces the most reliable outcomes in practice.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: The Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains. KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and progressive replacement to yield compact models that preserve much of teacher performance, but its effectiveness depends on dataset complexity, teacher quality, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Addressing pitfalls such as harmful teacher supervision on particular samples, degraded signals for low-frequency outputs, data unavailability, privacy concerns, and fairness requires targeted strategies (selective distillation, adapted teachers, self-distillation, generative replay, or tailored objectives).

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The approaches span soft-logit supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and adaptations for special settings such as low-precision inference, multimodal models, graph data, federated learning, and heterogeneous-device training. Empirical work shows KD can improve student accuracy, robustness, and latency while theoretical analyses connect KD to label smoothing and regularization effects. Best practice choices (which teacher signals to match, which samples or augmentations to use, and how to align heterogeneous inputs) materially affect outcomes. This synthesis summarizes known methods, insights about why KD helps, and practical considerations for deploying KD in real-world ML systems.

papers_seen.author: Avila
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Task‑Aware Toolbox — Powerful but Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. KD reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and deployment constraints. However, KD has clear limits — capacity and architecture mismatch, data scarcity and distribution shift, and the risk of propagating teacher errors or bias — so it is best used as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture co-design, and explicit fairness/privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller students. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals, synthetic data) and in protocol (offline, online, self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, data-free variants). Empirical results across vision, language, generation, and graph domains demonstrate that distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is carefully designed and combined with complementary compression techniques; however, success depends on factors such as teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes including bias transfer and degraded performance on rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also uses pretraining, architecture-aware design, and safeguards for privacy and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Gates
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Practices, Mechanisms, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile family of methods for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD techniques vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure), how teachers and students are arranged (offline, online, ensemble, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers), and whether distillation is combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD succeeds across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks but is context-sensitive: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, loss and mapping design, and deployment constraints. Practical distillation therefore requires task- and deployment-aware choices, and often additional techniques (data augmentation, feature projectors, adversarial objectives, or data-free synthesis) to close the gap to teachers while avoiding transferred errors or degraded handling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Christian
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practical Findings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller students. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when combined with deployment-aware design choices and complementary compression tools. However, realizing robust, fair, and privacy-preserving compressed models requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and method selection.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the last decade KD has expanded from matching teacher logits to a configurable set of signals and protocols (intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data‑free/federated variants). When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task‑aware design choices, KD enables favorable trade‑offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy. However, its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals and data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and distribution shift. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a central, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all solution.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under constraints of latency, memory, compute, or privacy. Methods range from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and specialized data strategies. KD has enabled strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks (classification, generation, translation, graph learning, and recommender systems) but requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors. Key practical themes include selecting appropriate distillation signals, handling teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatches, designing or synthesizing data when originals are unavailable, and integrating KD with complementary compression methods to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible approach to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, distillation can recover accuracy for lightweight architectures, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and transfer specialized properties (e.g., temporal, structural, or ensemble knowledge). However, distillation is not a panacea: its success depends on the choice of teacher, student architecture and capacity, the training protocol (including data augmentation and sample selection), and implementation details that affect optimization. When these factors are treated carefully, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, architecture design, quantization) and can be adapted to domain-specific needs such as federated learning, retrieval, and vision-language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). The field has developed a broad toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, and teacher-student co-training — that has been applied across vision, language, multimodal, detection, segmentation, and federated settings. Empirical work shows distilled models can often recover much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost; success depends on student capacity, alignment of inputs and layers, availability and nature of distillation data, and choices about what form of knowledge to transfer. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and task-aware adaptations; outstanding challenges include principled theory, reliable distillation under data or device heterogeneity and privacy constraints, transferring rare or structured outputs, and automating teacher/student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Distillation can transfer many types of knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive signals) and can be adapted to scenarios that lack original training data, require privacy guarantees, or demand task- and hardware-aware compression. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, architecture search, pretraining, or ensemble teaching), KD enables large reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving performance. Nevertheless, distillation can propagate biases and teacher artifacts and needs targeted remedies (feature-focused objectives, multi-teacher strategies, teacher annealing, or exposure to raw data) to avoid failure modes on rare phenomena. The literature demonstrates both the breadth of KD methods and concrete best practices to maximize effectiveness across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Robertson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when combined with task‑aware objectives and complementary compression techniques, but it must be integrated with targeted data, architectural, and fairness-aware practices to address limitations such as distribution shift, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency behavior loss, and bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for compressing large or ensemble deep models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of task performance. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure), how distillation is arranged (offline, online, multi- or self-distillation), and how data is used or synthesized; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture adaptations, KD supports deployments under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD produces strong empirical gains across modalities (vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, and generative models) but requires task-aware design—matching distilled signals to student capacity, coping with limited or mismatched data, and mitigating propagation of teacher errors—to be reliable in production.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Integrated Model Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, memory, and latency, but it is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on careful selection of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression primitives and privacy safeguards. Best practice treats KD as the configurable core of an end‑to‑end compression pipeline rather than as a standalone remedy.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably produces compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. KD succeeds across modalities when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student design are chosen for the target task and constraints, and its practical value is maximized when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. However, KD has concrete failure modes—teacher bias propagation, capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and degradation on rare or out-of-distribution phenomena—that require task‑aware engineering and integrated pipelines for deployment-grade results.

papers_seen.author: Travis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — Advocating Integrated Compression Pipelines for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, empirically validated approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models, enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. While KD reliably recovers much of teacher performance across modalities when carefully designed, it is context-sensitive: its success depends on choices of distillation targets, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Consequently, KD should be treated as the core component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation signals, architecture-aware adaptations, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Herring
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, many-to-many layer mappings, projector-based feature transforms, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis — enables large reductions in parameters and inference cost while often preserving much of teacher performance. Successful application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle data availability and privacy, and how to combine KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning and quantization. Remaining research challenges include principled theory for objective selection, reliable transfer under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Component of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of teacher functionality. KD methods have been adapted across modalities and tasks and can enable deployment under strict latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD has concrete failure modes tied to teacher quality, data availability, distribution shift, and architecture mismatch; achieving reliable outcomes requires integrating KD with complementary techniques and designing task-aware protocols that select what to transfer, how to synthesize or select data, and how to weight teacher signals.

papers_seen.author: Harrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically driven family of techniques to transfer knowledge from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Modern KD encompasses simple soft-target matching as well as richer objectives that imitate intermediate representations, attention patterns, relational structure, and contrastive signals; it is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation succeeds across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks when aligned to task objectives, teacher–student capacity, and available data, but it has well-documented failure modes (capacity mismatch, teacher bias propagation, domain shift, and scarce/private data) that motivate task-aware design, data strategies, and privacy-preserving or data-free approaches.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows KD methods often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. However, KD exhibits well-documented failure modes—capacity and architecture mismatch, transfer of teacher errors and biases, degraded long-tail behavior, and sensitivity to data regimes—that require complementary algorithmic and pipeline-level remedies. Treating KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression strategy (combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and careful data or privacy protocols) is the most reliable path to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Payne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster, or specialized student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A broad and practical toolbox has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free/zero-shot protocols, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search—that is applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative settings. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance when applied carefully, but success depends on student capacity, teacher design/quality, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices; important open problems remain in principled theory, fairness/privacy-aware protocols, heterogeneous and federated settings, and robust distillation for generative and structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Spencer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely successful family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost, but its reliability depends on task- and data-aware design choices, teacher–student alignment, and integration with complementary compression primitives. Responsible deployment requires explicit attention to data availability, distributional shift, rare-case behaviors, and fairness or privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable component of a compression pipeline and adapted to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints, KD reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on signal selection, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and integration with complementary compression methods; responsible use requires mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, low‑frequency degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best Used within Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applicable and practically effective toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD can recover much of teacher performance, enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, and be extended across logits, feature, attention, and data‑free paradigms. Its effectiveness, however, is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and selection of distillation data, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable, task‑aware component that must be combined with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies, and robustness/fairness safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but large deep models by transferring knowledge from larger or more complex models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). Across vision, speech, recommendation, retrieval, and NLP tasks, KD has been adapted into many forms—single- and multi-teacher schemes, data-free and federated variants, task-adaptive compression, and methods that target robustness, fairness, or cross-modal transfer. Empirical results show KD can yield large speed and size gains with modest performance loss and in some cases match or exceed teacher performance when combined with architectural or training strategies. Open challenges remain around teacher quality and heterogeneity, data availability, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, adversarial robustness, and deploying distillation in privacy-sensitive or resource-constrained environments.

papers_seen.author: Rosales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teachers into compact students. KD variants—ranging from logits and feature matching to relational, contrastive, and data-free protocols—have been demonstrated across vision, speech, and NLP to deliver favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. At the same time, KD’s success depends on teacher quality, signal choice, data regime, and careful training design, and it is most reliable when integrated with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a central, configurable element of any compression pipeline, but not as a standalone solution: use KD deliberately, combine it with other methods, and adopt practices that mitigate its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted and versatile family of methods for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal tasks. The literature converges on a toolbox of distillation objectives (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or generative approaches), multiple data regimes (full-data, few-shot/limited-data, and data-free/zero-shot), and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers most teacher performance and can act as both information transfer and regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, choice of transfer signals, and data availability. Remaining practical challenges include teacher–student mismatch, transfer of teacher errors or biases, preserving low-frequency and structured outputs, privacy- and federated-learning constraints, and automating task-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Barker

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD frequently produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful design choices for distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Lester
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically important family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, multimodal, and constrained-deployment settings, KD uses diverse transfer targets and training protocols to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals, student capacity, and data strategies to task and deployment constraints and on integrating KD with complementary compression methods and privacy-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Lucas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance, but outcomes are strongly context-dependent: they depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, choice of transfer signals and data regime, and explicit measures to avoid transferring teacher errors, biases, or fragile behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Stephens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied strategy for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teachers into compact students. Across modalities, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on the choice of distilled signals, teacher and student design, data availability, and integration with complementary compression techniques; awareness of practical failure modes such as capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, distribution shift, and transferred biases is essential. This synthesis summarizes what is known about KD methods, practical integrations with other compression approaches, representative applications, common limitations, and recommended design principles for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Galvan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical approach for transferring knowledge from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD variants and training protocols enable large reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. Real-world success depends on task- and capacity-aware choices of distillation signals, teacher–student co-design, data strategies (including data-free and federated variants), and combination with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is powerful but conditional: it frequently yields strong trade-offs in practice but requires careful treatment of teacher quality, data regimes, and robustness or fairness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically proven family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD offers a rich set of signals and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and self‑distillation, and data‑free or privacy‑aware variants—that can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD’s effectiveness is conditional: success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and distributional failures. Treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD reliably improves efficiency while preserving much teacher performance; treated as a turnkey solution, it risks suboptimal or unsafe outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, multimodal, and graph tasks. When combined with architecture-aware design, layer- and feature-level objectives, adversarial or relational losses, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, NAS), KD enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss and can sometimes improve generalization. KD also faces clear limits—teacher bias, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and optimization instability—that require task-aware curricula, multi-teacher or ensemble strategies, and careful selection of distilled signals. This paper argues that KD should be the first-line instrument in compression toolkits for deep learning and NLP, provided practitioners adopt principled protocols that address known failure modes and integrate KD with complementary methods for the target deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Juarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across vision, language, graphs, multimodal tasks and specialized settings (e.g., 3D detection, ranking, medical imaging), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data or synthetic alternatives are used; KD is most effective when used as a configurable component combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware training strategies.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. KD encompasses many targets and protocols and—when designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data, and complementary compression methods—regularly yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: careful protocol design, combination with pruning/quantization/architecture search, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and long‑tail behaviors are required for dependable real‑world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance; it is most effective when combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation, and hardware-aware design). The literature also highlights several persistent challenges — teacher and capacity mismatch, optimization and data limitations, privacy and distribution shift — and converges on practical strategies such as careful choice of distillation signals, layer alignment, multi-teacher or online protocols, and synthetic-data or data-free approaches to operate under constrained access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods span soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and variants that operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free regimes. Empirical work shows KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when carefully designed and often improves deployability under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practical success is context dependent: it requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, the availability and selection or synthesis of data, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Remaining needs include reliable distillation under distribution shift and data scarcity, principled guidance for signal and layer mapping, and methods that provably preserve fairness, robustness, and privacy in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Singleton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows KD methods often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. However, KD exhibits well-documented failure modes—capacity and architecture mismatch, transfer of teacher errors and biases, degraded long-tail behavior, and sensitivity to data regimes—that require complementary algorithmic and pipeline-level remedies. Treating KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression strategy (combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and careful data or privacy protocols) is the most reliable path to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Rose
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. KD encompasses many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free and privacy-aware variants). Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines appropriate distillation objectives with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies) and careful evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations across logits, features, attention and relational signals, enabling deployments under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and careful integration with complementary compression methods and robustness/fairness safeguards. Treating KD as a configurable, task‑aware element of an integrated compression pipeline yields the most reliable real‑world outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels — soft targets (logits), intermediate representations, attention and relational structure, and contrastive objectives — and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, pretraining, and architecture adaptation. Practical success is conditional on teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful optimization and evaluation to avoid propagating teacher artifacts, degrading rare-case behavior, or failing under distribution shift. The field shows strong empirical gains across vision, language, speech, recommendation, generative, and multimodal tasks, while open problems remain in theory, heterogeneous architectures, privacy-aware protocols, and robust transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Morris

Its strengths arise from a diverse set of distillation signals and training protocols that can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations; its practical value is greatest when KD is treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that also uses complementary techniques and task-aware data strategies.
